For example, Elon Musk's Starlink may sound like a good idea in peacetime, but relying on this in war would leave countries with fewer destroyed satellites away from chaos.
I mean, rogue actors are already using this to shut down hospitals or leak intelligence, and so it's only a matter of time before we see desperate or unethical governments adopt these methods.
And we're only talking about the conventional methods of disrupting a country's ability to fight.
I mean, even in peacetime, China and Russia have used social media to manipulate the people of foreign countries.

They could even stop a war before it starts by pushing anti-war sentiments and hit pieces on Facebook or TikTok, with state-owned platforms like TikTok having the very real potential to push propaganda and unrest around a country.
This is a new type of warfare that the world hasn't seen.
And once countries master this new type of social media warfare, they can then make entire populaces much more willing to fight, or sapping the strength of the enemy's will.
I mean, Russia and China have been practicing and building up their capabilities for years on this front, and it seems like the West has a lot of catching up to do.
But even all these present and future technologies ignore the elephant in the room, nuclear weapons.
If World War 3 becomes a total war, there's no saying how long it would take before nuclear weapons are used.
Mutually a sore destruction has kept countries from pushing the big red button for years.
But all of this goes out of the window during wartime.
If Xi, Putin or King Jermaine saw their regime crumbling around them, it's a big leap of faith to believe that they wouldn't turn to their nuclear arsenals.
But even with this threat, it's not hard to see wars still breaking out.
It will just look a lot different to those previous world wars.
With World War 3 potentially seeing much more limited front lines and much more emphasis placed on infrastructure disruption and economic pressure.
Both Russia and China's war goals encourage this model.
Both teams set on the occupation of specific countries, rather than some grand plan for world dominance.
Putin's Russia may not want to stop at Ukraine, but with the current pace things are going, any dreams of reuniting the Russian Empire won't come to fruition anytime soon.
And any greater European war would look much more like an expanded war on Ukraine, with Russia defending attacks from both Finland and other parts of Eastern Europe.
Likewise, it seems like China is set on taking Taiwan, but there isn't much reason to go beyond the one-China policy.
Although what can be accomplished through occupation is much easier to gain through trade dominance and economic pressure.
They would invade Taiwan, which would also have the effect of crippling the US's source of microchips, with things like microchips being the hidden war between the US and China right now.

From Taiwan and their artificial islands, China would be able to suffocate trade in the Pacific, and so a war would likely revolve around who can control the shipping lanes, with the US pulling in Japan, Australia and other allies, with the ground war likely being limited to Taiwan and the Korean Peninsula.
If China could establish regional dominance, they would be able to get all of the resources they need without outright invading Southeast Asia.

And even though the Chinese Navy did surpass the US Navy in size in 2020, the US still possesses a dwindling technological advantage, adding in both side allies, and it looks like China isn't really ready for a war just yet.
And unless America has other problems to worry about, a large-scale war in the Pacific would end very badly for the CCP, and could undo decades of work increasing their soft power over Asia.
Russia, on the other hand, poses a much more direct threat.
The EU would struggle to hold out against an overwhelming offensive.
But Russia would have to make quick and stable gains before the EU's economic superiority kicks in or before the US gets involved.
And this means that the real danger period for the West will come in the next few years.
And if the Chinese military can develop enough before Russia loses their edge, the US and the West could easily lose a war on two fronts.

title: One of These Countries Will Collapse In The Next Month
note: Country-by-country list structure with a Sri Lanka case study as template, a mid-film sponsor read, and a hopeful close.
lines: Since December of 2022, protests have overtaken Peru after a botched coup attempt and at least 55 people have died in the violence so far.
Meanwhile, across the world in Iran, over 500 people have been killed in the growing revolt against a theocratic government.
And in the past couple of years, countries and cities across the world have all erupted into flames.
Hong Kong, Bulgaria, Belarus and Venezuela all saw massive anti-government demonstrations.
And this was just 2020 alone.
On average, there are new anti-government protests every four days in 2020, and they've only gotten more common sense.
And it's not really hard to see why.

People across the world have had their lives ruined by both the pandemic, years of recessions, rampant corruption and political chaos, which are all the warning signs of an imminent collapse, a process which has already begun in the five countries we're going to be talking about soon.
To get a look at what might be in store for these unlucky nations, we only need to look so far as Sri Lanka as a warning sign.
You see, among the developing nations of South and Southeast Asia, Sri Lanka has been the hardest hit in recent years.
Coming off the back of a bitter civil war, the government seemed hopeful that they could bring Sri Lanka into the future.
They turned inwards, passing laws to focus the economy on making goods for domestic use rather than exports.
But more controversially, they took on massive amounts of debt in a grand rebuilding project.
And at first, this seemed to work.
In 2012, GDP growth rose to over 9% for the first time in years.
But as exports fell, the economy folded again and growth dropped.
So the government tried taking on more debt, hoping to kickstart the economy with infrastructure projects and a flood of foreign money.
But this failed as well.
The economy still didn't pick up as the national debt grew to ludicrous proportions.
and so in 2015, a newly elected government did little to stop the bleeding after their new economic plan failed to pass the parliament.

Tax increases and other changes to the economy were only successful in keeping inflation under control, but it never solved the deeper problems, with economic growth continuing to fall despite all of the government's attempts to reverse the decline.
And with the government continually changing to fight this problem, this led to even more economic chaos as the country's plans to get to the crisis got more and more confused.
Slowly, the situation was becoming dire and foreign debt rose to nearly 87% of the country's GDP.

But when the country needed a break, they got another kick in the teeth instead, with COVID bringing the whole country to a standstill, cutting off all of their economic growth when the country needed it the most.
Years of mismanagement brought the economy to its knees, and then COVID gave it the final coup de grace.
And so in just two years, Sri Lanka burned through nearly all of their foreign currency reserves, from over $7 billion to just $250 million.
And they were now importing $3 billion a year more than they exported, which was bleeding the country dry.
Eventually, the Sri Lankan people had enough, with widespread protests erupting across the country.
And all the attempts at a last-minute fix only made everything so much worse.

The government tried to ban fertiliser imports to encourage farmers to use domestic products, but this led to massive crop failures and massive food shortages, which was then accompanied by massive inflation, spiking to over 50% as well as skyrocketing prices across the board.

And so in May of 2021, the government defaulted on their debts and then promptly collapsed, with Sri Lankan society ceasing to function properly, as fuel shortages led to nationwide bans and daily power cuts became the norm.

causing the Sri Lankan president to eventually flee to Singapore, and the new interim government only lasting three days before it was ousted by the people after they occupied the presidential palace.
People's power has won.
Now we have forced these two leaders, President Gautabai Rajapaksa and Prime Minister Ranit Vikramasinghe, they've agreed to resign, and that is a great victory for us.
And now today, the road to recovery looks long and arduous for the long-suffering citizens of Sri Lanka.
Even with debt restructuring and foreign investment, it would take a very long time before the country can get back on its feet.
Stagnating wages and high costs promise years of suffering, but in lots of countries, the chaos has only just begun.
And if you thought Sri Lanka's government seemed ineffective and corrupt, just wait until we see Peru.
Protests and riots have rocked the country ever since December when the president tried to dissolve parliament and then got removed from office.
When he was arrested just days later, it only made everything so much worse.
And of course, this isn't an isolated incident.
Peru's own internal struggles have been bubbling away for years, and possibly the biggest problem is corruption.
With high levels of economic growth and very low amount of debt, Peru has seen a major economic boom over the last 20 years.
And whilst poverty rates have fallen because of this, they haven't fallen nearly enough.
Pervasive and deeply set corruption has seen the majority of the spores fall into the hands of the rich and powerful.
Well-off residents of the capital Lima have seen all of the benefits, while the rest of the country has had to endure a 20% poverty rate.
But corruption isn't just an economic problem, it is spread into every layer of Peruvian society.
When it came to COVID, for example, Peru had the worst mortality rate in the world.
And corruption meant that millions that should have gone into healthcare went towards bribes and kickbacks instead.
And all of this led to the lowest rates of trust towards the governments in Latin America, only just behind Haiti.
And it's these years of corruption that's choked Peru's rural regions and has made the people resentful.
Meanwhile, in the capital, lots of people still supported the current regime and its centralized power.
This divide has horned to Peru in politics for years, but in recent years, the nations have only gotten more polarized.
A string of election scandals, vote rigging and Peru's classic corruption led to a political crisis that lasted for years, all building up to the 2021 election.
Then from seemingly out of nowhere, The left-wing politician, Pedro Castillo, gained a massive following by tackling the key issues of corruption and poverty.
The first result was too close, leading to a separate runoff election for the presidency between the two leading candidates.
Castillo won that by an incredibly slim majority of just 50.13%.
Peru's electoral authority has finally named socialist Pedro Castillo as the country's next president.
Castillo has won the election by a margin of nearly 44,000 votes, beating his right-wing rival Keiko Fujimori in the third bid for the presidency.
But even though he was now the president, he had no control over the government.
The real power lies with Congress, which is still mostly made up of his rivals.
Soon it became clear that Castillo couldn't deliver on any of his promises.
Then he got caught up in a corruption scandal and failed to deal with the rising cost of Peru's poorest citizens.
He was just another politician it seemed.
Seeing no other options, Castillo moved to seize power by dissolving Congress.
But it was a desperate and ill-fated attempt.
And after his cabinet members resigned and Castillo tried to flee to Mexico, he was promptly arrested.
which eventually led to months of protests which are still happening today.
I mean recently it's gotten so bad that Machu Picchu was closed indefinitely because of the violence and for now the government has been able to stay in power by fighting and killing the protesters.
But if this chaos continues it won't survive for very long.
Even before COVID and the recessions Peru was struggling to keep itself together but these outside pressures have pushed Peru to the brink of collapse.
Peru's government clearly doesn't have a mandate from the people instead they're keeping control through violence and bloodshed.
Myanmar gives us a window into what Peru's current problems could quickly devolve into if left unchecked.
You see, ever since they wrestled with independence from the British, Myanmar has been under the yoke of a military dictatorship.
ship.
And over the last few decades, they have controlled Mianima's government, either indirectly or by force, smothering any democratic reforms wherever they spring up.
And throughout this period, Mianima's people have been given glimpses of real democracy, most recently in the 2020 election.
Funnily enough, when people were finally given a choice, the pro-democracy party won in an absolute landslide.
And so very quickly, the military realized they were losing their grip on power.
And so they played nice at first, telling the public that they would honor the constitution and step back from power.
But after just a few months, a coup was underway.
Black fans and armored cars moved in to arrest key members of the pro-democracy party, including the new president.
And once they were in power, the new junta declared martial law.
Banned gatherings of more than five people, shut down social media and announced a new emergency government.
And needless to say, the people weren't all too happy about this.

Immediately protests erupted across the nation and in the larger cities, but the military cracked down hard, which is why after a few months of violence and bloodshed, the crowds eventually died down and disappeared.
But the resistance hadn't gone away completely, it just moved underground.
And ever since the coup, young freedom fighters have launched a guerrilla war from the jungles in the north.
And this war is running alongside the junta's other military operations in the east, where has been oppressing and massacring a Muslim minority called the Rohingya.
You see, over the course of the coup, over 2,500 people have died at the hands of Maynama's police and soldiers.
And because of the resulting civil war, over 600,000 people have been forced to flee their homes.
But this political violence overshadows other deep problems in Maynama, like poverty.
The junta is only able to keep themselves in power by impoverishing their people, a tactic which they've perfected over decades of rule.
This is why nearly half of Myanmar's people live below the poverty line, and this number is still rising.
Meanwhile, the military junta have turned to other means to finance their wars.
The junta have turned to opium to turn a profit, with their exports of the drug doubling in 2022.
And you see previously, farmers were incentivized to grow other crops despite being less valuable, which is all amounting to a humanitarian disaster in Myanmar.
And unless the people can overthrow the military dictatorship, things are only going to get so much worse.
But that's unlikely to happen in the near future without significant international pressure, something which has been lacking in recent months.
But to anyone watching, Mayanama is very close to collapse, and we can only hope that the government will break down before it can erode the will of the people.
But whilst Mayanama's freedom movement seems to have calcified into a long war of attrition, Iran's democratic wave has only just gotten started.
Similar to Mayanama, Iran has been under the thumb of a totalitarian regime for decades now.
Ever since the late 70s after a violent revolution, Iran has been governed as an extreme theocracy.
Women's rights were ground down to nothing, whilst a small majority of religious leaders took all the power for themselves.
And over the years, this regime has become one of the most oppressive in the world by restricting basic rights and executing anybody that they want.
Now, there have been some major protests in the past, but none of them were a credible threat to the regime's security.
For example, in 2009, millions took to the streets to protest a rigged election, but the movement failed to gain any real momentum with the working class people.
Then, in the late 2010s, more protests were held over major economic problems, but this time the middle classes weren't very engaged.

It was only until 2022 that we finally saw a united front, Outrage over the killing of a 22-year-old woman in September for not covering her hair led to violence in the streets and the regime cracking down with lethal force.
But this only incentivized more protests, and soon enough, every corner of the nation was lit up by the fires of the unrest.
People from all walks of life took to the streets to protest the lack of women's rights in particular, alongside the government's other grievers' crimes.
Now, Iran hasn't been sluggish in their response either, doubling down on suppression, arrests and murder.
In total, the Iranian government has killed over 500 people in an effort to squash the protests.
But right now, it's not really working.
Protests are still going on internationally.
It's even gotten to the point where the former president is calling for Iran's government to give in to their demands.
But the government doesn't just have a growing revolution on their hands.
They're also surrounded by enemies on all sides.
Bitter relations with the West, among many other things, have made Iran an international pariah.
They've been under heavy sanction for years, which has severely restricted the country's economy.
Covid also played its own part, of course.
And now the protests have seen social media shutdowns across the nation.
And this will affect tons of businesses which rely on the internet to market themselves.
On top of this, they've been in a cold war with Saudi Arabia for years, who want nothing more than to topple the Iranian government.
Now, it's a question of survival for Iran, but they won't go down easily.
And even if the regime does fall, it doesn't necessarily promise a brighter future.
A regime change in Iran would be incredibly likely to lead to civil war and chaos.
We've already seen the protests take its course in Libya and Syria, but for lots of Iran's people, it's a risk worth taking.
However, by looking at all these different countries, it's clear that COVID and economic pressures have pushed all of these corrupt regimes to the brink.
But our last country is being faced with a different threat, water shortages.
What should be a historical problem is set to become one of the largest issues of the 2020s.
And no country knows this better than Egypt.
For the past year in Egypt, the country has been incredibly dry.
And there's already droughts all over the world.
But you see, in Egypt, the problem is so much worse.
95% of Egypt's 102 million people live next to and depend on the River Nile.
And Ethiopia right now is damming it up at the source.
with their new mega dam only recently being built, and it's still getting expanded upon today.
Sudan, which once acted as a buffer between Ethiopia and Egypt, has also been swayed to Ethiopia's side on the matter.
And so once it's finished, Ethiopia will have full control over Egypt, being able to turn off their economy and put their people in danger at will.
The dam could plunge the country into famine.
It would take an ironclad regime to survive this extraterrestrial threat without collapsing.
And Egypt's current government is far from that.
Ever since the military government took power in a coup 10 years ago, they've been on shaky ground, desperately trying to turn the economy around.
And to do this, they took out massive loans, but it was never enough.
And so like Sri Lanka, more and more loans kept coming in.
But as creditors got nervous, the interest rates skyrocketed.
And then the hole continued to get deeper.
And now they're dealing with over $50 billion in debt to foreign creditors, triple what it was in 2013.
And all of this has left 60% of Egypt's population close to or under the poverty line.
They won't be able to take much more, and most blame the military government.
Their tight control of the economy has stunted it, placing it in a terrible debt spiral.
And harsh cuts to public spending have made people's lives measurably worse.
And yet nothing has been done to stop the crisis, with the government even spending sorely needed funds on vapid mega-projects like a new capital.

Although this is a ploy to give the regime a more secure base away from the crowds that toppled the last one, it's not even close to completion yet, despite the massive amounts of money that have been thrown away.
And new promises of foreign bailouts announced last month came with few conditions for economic reform, meaning they only promise a delay to impending economic chaos.
And with inflation at 20% annually, and this figure rising, it remains to be seen how an extra few billion will solve the problem.
And all of this is now putting Egypt's relatively new autocrats in an incredibly fragile position.
And if these problems go unchecked, Egypt's government will completely collapse.

title: Why Elon Musk Is A Fraud
note: Company-and-founder rise-and-fall: origin, Musk takeover, boom years, then a catalogue of causes for the 2022 decline, with a mid-film sponsor read.
sections: Founding by Eberhard and Tarpenning, Musk joins
Founders pushed out, Musk takes control
Musk's online persona, Twitter posts, Dogecoin
lines: Tesla has broken records in their race to dominate the electric car market.
Their charming CEO, Elon Musk, became the richest man in the world, with his jewel in the crown, Tesla, revolutionising the car industry.
And after growing by 800% in just a year in 2021, Tesla has now plummeted straight back down again.

And Elon Musk, who once stood so tall, has started to lose the support of the public and a large part of his fortune, with the quality of Tesla going down the plug hole, with recent reports that Tesla's new cars can spontaneously combust.
And in addition to this, competitors are now finally beginning to catch up and even overtake Tesla in key areas.
And so with their lead dwindling, questions are being asked about Tesla's role in the future of electric cars.
For how much longer are they going to overtake the competition?
And where will Tesla be in the next decade?
You see, if we go back 20 years ago, Elon Musk was never there from the very beginning.
Instead, Tesla was initially created by two men, Martin Eberhard and Mark Tappening, who both saw an opportunity.
You see, back in 2003, electric cars were more of a curiosity than a product.
And there were two reasons for this.
The batteries and the reputation.
The first problem was practical.
The current battery technology just wasn't up to scratch for an electric car with an adequate range.
They needed to use much newer lithium-ion batteries, but they kept exploding when put into laptops and other electronics.
And this then fed into the second problem of reputation.
That and the fact that the only electric cars that had made a dent so far were all really ugly and utilitarian.
And whilst Honda's EV Plus and GM's EV1 had a certain charm, they just weren't exciting.
But where some people saw problems, Martin and Mark saw an opportunity, because they were both highly skilled electrical engineers, and they knew the technology existed to solve the battery problem.
All they needed was time and funding, and this is where Elon Musk came in.
Before the company had grown out of the ideas phase, Musk was guiding development and putting down money, contributing $6.5 million of the initial $7.5 million that Tesla began with.
But how did Musk find out about this, and where did he get the money to do this?
Well, of course, Musk's career began way before Tesla.
Throughout his childhood, his father's personal fortune grew exponentially off the back of a stake in an emerald mine.
They couldn't even close their safe at times because it was so stuffed with money.
And so by using this early money, Musk would use his entrepreneurial genius to found a company called Zip2, one of his first major successes.
And after the $300 million sale of the company, Musk personally netted $22 million for his share.
But this was just the start because Musk made his real money from PayPal with a buyout of his shares giving him at least $150 million and possibly much, much more.
And so by the early 2000s, Musk was in his early 30s and had hundreds of millions of dollars.
But this just wasn't enough.
He wanted more.
He's already beginning his plans to colonize space with SpaceX.
But Musk then saw another massive opportunity.
And this was with Tesla.
After meeting with Martin and Mark, Musk was convinced of their success.
He could bankroll solving the first problem with the battery.
But the reputation part was a tricky problem to solve.
However, the team came up with a solution.
Their first car wouldn't be entry level or even designed for mass marketing.
It was going to be a sports car.
And this move was both genius and necessary.
Because even with millions of dollars, Tesla was still miles away from having the scale to make a mass consumer car.
Plus, a sports car would help shake off the geeky image that came with the territory.
And understanding this is key to understanding Tesla today, because it was this emphasis on the reputation of Tesla that would become one of the biggest problems that we see today.
But at the time, this was groundbreaking, and the first Tesla car was born.
And so by using new techniques to develop a safe, efficient battery, Tesla was finally ready to begin production.
And this is how the Tesla Roadster was born.
The initial demos and launch of the Tesla Roadster were a massive hit.
there was a huge buzz over the potential of the car, and everyone loved the look and the design, much of which had been contributed by Musk.
But it was going to be a long road until they reached the mass market and started shipping some real numbers.
It would take years before they had a solid, predictable revenue stream.
So like any other tech startup, Tesla relied completely on investments to stay afloat.
In 2006, Tesla raised another $13 million in venture capital.
Then a few months later, they raised another $40 million from other investors.
A year later, this number was now over $100 million.
Musk was also contributing from his personal hoard, with over $70 million of his personal fortune going straight into Tesla.
But even this was barely enough at times.
It just cost so much to develop the economy of scale required to develop and release a mass market car, especially one that relied on new and relatively unproven technology.
It was also during this time that Musk cemented his hold on the company, and everything wasn't smooth within the company.

The founders were having big disagreements with Musk, which is why Tesla was running through a slew of different CEOs and board members, but none of them really stuck, which eventually resulted in both Martin and Mark leaving within months of each other and taking significant shares of the company with them.
Other controlling parties were pruned in a classic startup power struggle.
There was even a legal battle over who could be considered as a founder, among many, many other issues.
But once the dust eventually settled, Elon Musk was left at the head of the company and was now responsible for turning their buckets of potential into reality.
As for the company itself, Tesla was now starting to make a name for themselves selling the Roadster, but they would only ever make and sell 2,500 units.
Instead, it was their next project, the Model S, that was the reason so many people were betting hundreds of millions of dollars on Tesla.
In 2009, the first prototype was shown to the public, and three years later, they were on the market, all to massive acclaim.
And these weren't budget cars by any means, with an entry-level price of around $50,000.
But they were still accessible to normal people.
And once production finally started in 2012, they were only making around 15 to 20 cars a week.
But in just a few years, this had risen to over $1,000 per week.
And this was all because the Model S was such a huge success.
It was genius, it revolutionized the electric car market, and there was now so much demand for Tesla that the company now was starting to issue pre-orders.
Tesla even innovated in other small ways, like offering home delivery, something which other companies are only now catching up with.
Regardless, it was the cars that mattered, and people loved the Model S.
Described as giving a phenomenal driving experience when it was released in 2012, and so the buzz only continued to grow over the next few years, as Tesla showed people the future of electric cars.
And by 2014, Tesla had sold over 2,500 Model S cars.
Then a year later, Tesla sold 10,000 and swept the design awards after significantly improving their batteries and adding a boatload of new features.
However, before the success, Tesla's early days were very tough.
The company only survived on investments, with people always predicting its downfall.
And at one point, the company was even just a few days away from bankruptcy.
Essentially, the company was bleeding money like crazy and just, if we didn't solve these problems in a very short period of time, we would die.
and it was extremely difficult to solve them.
How close to death did you come?
Within single legit weeks.
But the success of the Model S emboldened investors in Elon Musk himself and their next release was set to change the entire industry.
In 2016, Musk announced that Tesla were making a new car, the Model 3 sedan.
It was going to be Tesla's first car that was truly for the mass market.

Because of new features like a lower price tag and the fact that Tesla very rarely released a new car, pre-orders flooded in, with Tesla receiving 180,000 pre-orders in just the first 24 hours after release.
But the release of the Model 3 was the beginning of a new alarming trend in Musk's running of the company.
You see, he boldly promised that Tesla would be able to produce over 200,000 cars, all in the second half of 2017 alone.

But once push came to shove, Tesla only managed a quarter of this figure, and the financial world wasn't kind to the company after this wild overestimation either, causing Tesla to lose $12 billion in value during the fallout.
But this was seemingly just a momentary blip on the radar for Tesla's growth, as every new car wasn't just a sale, it was proof that Tesla's concept for the future of electric cars was the future.
Because before, electric cars had been an untested concept in the world of cars, and they weren't anywhere near close to breaking into the mainstream.
But this all changed with Tesla, who made the public not just only accept them, but made them desirable.
High quality and self-driving features that were far more advanced than the competition cemented this image.
But it wasn't just the image that Tesla were building on, their first gigafactory was finally ramping up their production.
Plans had begun years ago, but by 2018, there were over 7,000 people working and building Tesla batteries and other components.
And once it's fully completed, it will have the largest footprint in the world.
And this is just the first massive factory.
More are under construction in New York, Shanghai and Berlin just for starters.
And this massive demand for Tesla combined with the production ramping up meant that there was a very real threat that Tesla would take on the whole car industry by storm.
And when the world realized this, people started throwing all of their money at Tesla like there was no tomorrow.
In 2018, Tesla's stock was worth around $20, rising to over $30 in the next two years.
But in 2020, the stock went to the moon, nearly breaking the $300 mark in the first weeks of 2021.
The pandemic had been incredibly kind to Tesla, much kinder than almost any other company, which continued to lead to massive demand for the stock and the company in general.
But just over the last year, Tesla's stock prices collapsed as only 36%.
And this is bad news for almost everyone, whether we know it or not.
Now a lot of this huge jump in how people valued the company was justified by their sales figures and their overall potential, but a large part of it was down to Elon Musk himself.
You see, Elon had always dreamt big, and his vision and internet gave him billions, and society rewarded his overambition time and time again, so why not push it a little further?
It was most visible in his online presence.
As well as furiously sh** posting on Twitter, Musk also made his political views and his opinions much more well known.
But for all the hits, there were a few misses as well.

For example, in July of 2018, Musk famously insulted a rescue worker after his ludicrous idea of a custom-built rescue submarine was called out, with Musk actually calling this rescue worker a pedophile, and was later forced to take back the accusation after it became clear that he really, really wasn't, later resulting in a massive defamation case, which, to be fair, Elon actually won.
But all in all, this was a publicity failure.
Then, just a month later, Musk made a much more serious mistake when he tweeted about his plans to buy a publicly-owned Tesla stock at $420 a share.
Predictably, Tesla's stock rose massively as a result, as did Elon's personal wealth.
But when it turned out that there was no concrete plan to buy Tesla stock, everything fell apart.
Now, to many, it seemed like a premeditated scheme to tamper with stock prices, and the legal battle over the fiasco is still raging to this day.
But despite the negative press coverage, the internet was still gripped by Musk fever.
His Tony Stark-esque image of the genius billionaire was contagious, and for every detractor there were legions of fanboys ready to defend him from any criticism.
He even sent Tesla into space, with images of the stunt gripping the internet for weeks after.
And this publicity extended to his other companies as well.
Whenever Elon's popularity rose, it brought up the stock prices of his companies with it.
And as Musk fever reached its height in 2020 and 2021, so did Tesla's stock price rising to $400 a share.
But Elon wasn't just having an effect on his own companies.
His ability to mess with the financial markets extended far outside of his direct control.
And this was perfectly illustrated by Dogecoin.
In 2021, Elon Musk made one tweet about Dogecoin and its value increased by 20% the following day.
And then when Musk announced that it could be used to pay for certain Tesla products, it rose by another 15% again.
Just his endorsement alone had added billions to the meme coins value.
Which to be honest should have been a warning to people.
A tweet shouldn't be the basis of billions of dollars in value being lost or gained.
And it obviously wasn't going to last, with Dogecoin now languishing at less than 10 cents each.
A far cry from its almost $1 value.
But in a way, Dogecoin's rise and fall would be mirrored by Tesla itself.
Throughout 2021, Tesla's stock price kept on rising.
And it looked like that good fortune was going to keep on rolling until it didn't.
Over 2022, Tesla slowly lost its value as a stock and as a company.
Then halfway through the year, it really started to tank.
May and June saw stock prices drop by $100, and by September they were dropping again.
But this time, it was going to be steep and sustained, with Tesla's value dropping by 70% during 2022, one of the largest drops it's ever seen.
You see, Tesla's meteoric rise had briefly made Elon Musk the richest man in the world.
However, this title dissolved away when the drop happened.
And so Tesla and Elon Musk were left asking themselves, what happened here?
Lots of people chalked Tesla's failure solely up to Elon Musk's of shenanigans.
However, the answer, of course, is way more complicated than this.
The first problem for Tesla was simple to diagnose, but incredibly hard to address.
And this problem being that they were losing their market share.
You see, in 2020, Tesla's market share was hovering at around 80%, with the company dominating the electric car market.
But now this figure has fallen to 65%, and it's still going down.
And whilst one of Tesla's greatest achievements was breaking the stigma surrounding electric cars, they have inadvertently opened up the market again.
And whilst their innovations bore them years in the spotlight, it won't carry the monopoly forever, just like Uber's experience today.
And now that other car companies have released electric cars reminiscent of Tesla's features, and at a lower price, Tesla is now losing their market share fast.
They're losing out on a world of consumers who want an electric car, but can't shell out the 50,000 plus it takes just to get the base model of Tesla.
There are plans to release a new budget friendly Tesla, but they're still just plans.
We might not see it for years, but the competition has already got their foot in the door.
Ford and Hyundai have both muscled in on Tesla's game.
It'll be nearly impossible for Tesla to keep their dominance over the next few years.
And when the market eventually becomes oversaturated, it'll be even harder for Tesla to justify the higher price points.
But Tesla still has the technological edge, right?
Well, not exactly.
Recently, we've seen a whole host of mistakes, bugs, and glitches from Tesla software.
Currently, they've rolled out a new self-driving system designed for city driving.
It's meant to be able to navigate complicated intersections and should be able to recognize traffic lights and other road systems.
But it's still just a beta version.
Real-world tests have found the system lacking.
And the fact that it's only open to drivers who pass a safety exam and stay alert at all times is a good safety feature, but it betrays how unsteady this really is.
Meanwhile, Mercedes-Benz's new self-driving system is miles ahead of Tesla's open beta, despite the fact that it still hasn't been released yet.
And yet Mercedes has achieved level 3 of autonomy, a far more advanced self-driving system than Tesla's beta system, which is still just level 2.
And whilst Mercedes-Benz are the first company to pull ahead of Tesla, they most likely won't be the last.
Quality has also played havoc on Tesla's future.
The past few years haven't been kind on Tesla's image, with tons of examples of public failures.
Like for example when Elon Musk tested the new Tesla truck's unbreakable glass windows by hitting them with a bat that completely broke on stage.
And whilst this was funny and wasn't too damaging for Tesla, some of the other incidents haven't been very lighthearted.
I mean just recently a Tesla spontaneously caught fire whilst driving on the freeway.
It took firefighters 22,000 litres of water before the fire even went out.
All due to how flammable the battery was once it got going.
And this wasn't the first time.
In September of 2022, another Tesla fire took around 90,000 litres to put out.
Now I'm not saying that your average Tesla is catching on fire, but it has been happening much more often.
And a strange coincidence is that the quality of Tesla's cars are dropping after plunging stock prices forced Tesla to lower prices by 10-13%.
In 2021, Elon Musk had to apologise for quality concerns, saying that the criticisms were accurate.
And since then, not much has changed, with a viral video in November of 2022 showing part of the car coming off when pulled on or wobbling when touched.
And just when you thought it couldn't get any worse, Tesla is infamous for treating its workers like garbage.
I mean, just a few months ago, a whistleblower who worked in one of Tesla's giga factories came out with allegations of workplace harassment, constant health and safety hazards, and even wage theft.
One worker claimed that his boss forged certificates for their workers, depriving them of essential training to save time and money.
Another said that employees were forced to work on the roof at night without any proper lighting and without any safety mask, despite working next to industrial chimneys.
Tesla's also been in hot water for allegedly telling their employees not to discuss their pay with each other, which is also against labor laws.
And every news story is another hit to Tesla's spotty reputation.
But even with all of the accusations and evidence piling up, Tesla's reputation has suffered the most from Elon Musk's embarrassing botched takeover of Twitter.
And recently Elon's reputation as an innovator and a genius businessman has been under fire for his poor handling of Twitter.
Now it hasn't by any means been a complete failure of course, and you have to respect how Elon Musk turned around Twitter's policy on free speech.

In addition to his releasing of the Twitter files, exposing how much they've been cloning with governments on censorship and promotion, any move towards the truth should always be praised, but it's impossible to deny the awful public perception of the rest of what's happened.
First, the deal to buy Twitter took years, and involved a long and public legal battle, which isn't the best start.
And once it was finally coming to a close, Elon walked into Twitter's main office holding a sink, making a pun about it, then proceeding to fire 50% of the workforce.
finishing off his debut by having a long public Twitter argument with his employees and firing whoever called him out.

And whilst I have to agree with Elon Musk on a lot of things about Twitter, the whole blue checkmark saga just led to more chaos and ridicule to the company, resulting in Elon Musk posting a poll asking whether he should step down as CEO, with 57% voting yes.
And so whilst all of this was going on, two things were happening.
Both Musk's reputation fell to tatters after every scandal, and Tesla's stock price also kept falling.
And this is why it's getting more and more certain that Tesla will have a dominant place in the future of electric cars, as their falling market share is symptomatic of an eroding monopoly.
And whilst 65% of market share is still in an incredibly strong position, this position is fading very fast.
The competitors have numerous advantages now as well.

Being a faceless corporation might have hurt when Musk's reputation was a good thing for Twitter, but now that it's swung the other way, other car companies won't have to worry about the problems that come with personal reputation dominating people's perceptions.
And when they crop up, controversies can be dealt with much easier and fade from the public eye faster if there isn't a face and character to associate with it.
Corporations always get away with a lot more than people, and Tesla's competitors also have much more experience and infrastructure to produce cars on a larger scale.
And now that electric cars are finally making their mark on the wider market, these advantages will matter a whole lot more than they did before.
And lots of people expect electric cars to dominate in the ride-sharing Uber market.
In fact, they already are in lots of places, with nearly all of London's black cabs being electric now.

But Tesla's high-cost, middling quality cars will struggle to make a dent in an industry that values reliability and price above everything else, which is the opposite of Musk's public perception and Tesla's recent scandals.
On the other hand, a successful breakthrough into the rental and ride-sharing market might not do Tesla any favours in the long run either.
Plus, if the electric car market doesn't take off, the competitors have their own cars to fall back on.

But Tesla doesn't have this luxury and is much more vulnerable to changes in the market, and considering the wild fluctuations of gas prices, traditional cars might still have decades left as the cheaper and more convenient option.
The revolution of self-driving cars seemed to cement Tesla's place at the top of the car industry, considering their leading role with technology.
But now that they've been overtaken, or at least caught up with, it's no guarantee of safety anymore.
And so the future of Tesla is fraught with potholes.
From losing the technological race, to exposing cars, to Elon Musk becoming a liability, there are just so many problems that Tesla now has to deal with.
And we've already seen how overvalued the company already was from the massive drops in the stock price.
And this is why in the next few years, Tesla's position could get a whole lot worse.
Thank you.

title: This May Be The Real Reason Why China Is Sending Spy Balloons
note: Event-driven explainer: build-up, a chronological incident, motive speculation, shoot-down, and a historical-parallel warning.
sections: Build-up: trade war to second Cold War
Balloon spotted and crosses the US
lines: One balloon caused panic, hysteria and filled the news for weeks.
The Chinese spy balloon got a full tour of the US's missile silos, air defences and other military installations.
But this whole Chinese spy balloon scandal is just so much worse than it seems.
And it marks a grave chapter in our new Cold War.
A Cold War which could very soon escalate into a full-scale conflict which threatens human civilization.
And now that it's been announced by the US government that the balloon may have carried an explosive payload, questions are being asked about the weakness of the US's slow response.
And so what really happened here?
And why is this story so important?
Well, just a week before the incident occurred, things were looking bleak.
But there was still some hope.
You see, it all began with Trump's trade war, a series of sanctions and tariffs aimed at gaining the economic upper hand against China.
But what was at first an economic conflict soon spread into other areas.
For example, China's brutal subjugation of Hong Kong's democracy left a very bitter taste in the West's mouth, as did new information about China's crimes against the Uyghurs.
And when China upped their aggression against Taiwan, the US responded with threats of intervention and war.
With Biden recently announcing that the US would protect Taiwan in the event of invasion, and now some US generals are predicting a coming war in as little as two years.
And so in a very short span of time, uneasy relations have shifted to a second Cold War, and things are heating up fast.
And that's where things were at the beginning of 2023.
But there was still some light at the end of the tunnel.
The US Secretary of State, Antony Blinken, was meant to attend a summit in China to cool relations.
He stated that the meeting was the perfect opportunity to establish, quote, guardrails to prevent tensions from erupting into war.

The CCP seemed welcoming of the opportunity to clear the air, with Xi Jinping ready to meet the American delegation over the weekend, and it was hoped that the two nations would soon simmer down this Cold War and skip straight to the peace summits.
The meeting was meant to get the ball rolling on a possible de-escalation of both countries.
But then just a few days before the planned visit, people in the US suddenly spotted an odd-looking object in the sky.
Claims that it was a UFO were quickly disproven after the US announced it was in fact a spy balloon, which they had been tracking since it was spotted over Alaska.
Estimated flight patterns placed the blame squarely at China's door, and at first they were almost apologetic, although they did insist it was a weather balloon, which had flown off course.
And whilst all of this was going on, the balloon just kept on going.
First in Montana, it flew over the missile silos and nuclear sites, often fully visible from the ground.
One site that the balloon exposed was the Maelstrom Air Force Base, which has around 150 intercontinental missile silos, as well as other vital military installations.
And so people were just powerless as they watched the 60-meter-tall Goliath cross the skies, hoovering up all of the US's military secrets.
And so what did the government do?
Well, they did nothing, silently watching the airspace be violated.
So what was going on here?
Well, first we can establish that this was clearly an intentional move.
Balloons navigate by lowering and raising their altitude, letting them take advantage of wind direction to move.
And so you see, the balloon had every opportunity to reverse its course, but instead, it flew directly towards the US.
So why did China send the balloon in the first place?
Well, here's a few possible motives.
First is the obvious reason that it could gain valuable intel on the USA's defense capabilities.
But beyond that, it was incredibly embarrassing for the US and the Biden administration.
Every minute that the balloon stayed in the sky proved the US's unreadiness and indecision.

It also could have been a demonstration of China's technological dominance, highlighting the weakness in what was thought to be the most powerful military in the world, surpassing the US's sophisticated defense system with a simple balloon.
However, a third and much more sinister motive is that China wanted to sabotage any chance of reconciliation.
I mean, why else would they take such a brazen and reckless move against the US?
Whilst the US was mulling over these questions, the balloon just kept on going.
After floating over Montana, it kept heading southeast over South Dakota and Nebraska.
It was next sighted over Kansas, two days after the first sighting.
and by now the balloon had crossed over half of the continental United States.
And this was when the announcements started flowing in as both of the superpowers established their adversarial positions.
And the worst news was yet about to hit.
America's Secretary of State, Antony Blinken, cancelled the summit.
He also called the spy balloon an irresponsible act on part of China.
So Beijing responded by saying that the incident had been hyped up to smear China.
The rhetoric was suddenly getting more and more aggressive.
But even though the balloon had been gathering data for days, the Biden administration decided not to shoot it down.
The reason they claimed was to avoid unnecessary damage.
But the fact that it stayed in the sky for so long is an embarrassment on the US government's behalf.
The US also claims that they had been tracking it since it was discovered over Alaska.
So it was never an issue of time.
So as you'd guess, Republicans would quit to launch into attacks on the Biden administration for their inaction.
One even called it a catastrophic spectacle.
But then the news came out that during the Trump administration, there had been three separate Chinese balloon incidents.
Another had also entered US airspace before Biden was elected.
Ex-Trump officials stated they were never briefed.
But perhaps this was just an excuse to shift blame.
But regardless of politics, all of this made the US as a country look even more ridiculous.
But it does beg the question of why this is the first time we're hearing about this.
Does the US usually overlook these spy balloons, letting them crisscross the country at will?
I mean, US officials have stated that the balloon can't get any more intel than a satellite could.
But as they haven't analysed the records, they can't really know this for certain.
And if this claim was actually true, why would China send the balloon in the first place?
It seems unlikely that the balloon wouldn't give China any new information whatsoever, even after conducting a full trip over the USA.
There are other less expensive ways of causing a diplomatic incident as well, trying to could have just cancelled the summit themselves.
So obviously there's much more to what's going on than we could possibly know at this point.
It could have been the fact that this was spotted by regular people, causing the whole incident in the first place.
And so once people were aware of its existence, the US hand was forced.

Regardless, the US went from tolerating these spy balloons to cancelling diplomatic meetings and ramping up tensions, implying that the US government might have wanted an excuse to keep tensions high as well.
A divided world could be of some geopolitical benefit.
An increased threat from China means that the US's allies are much more likely to let the American military set up their bases, for example.
However, the plot thickened when another high-altitude balloon was spotted, this time hovering over Latin America.
The US announced its presence on Friday, which was confirmed by Colombian officials a day later.
China later claimed ownership for this one as well, but said that this one was yet another weather balloon that flew off course.
And even with other evidence, it might have been a tiny bit plausible that the US balloon could simply have been a weather balloon.
But now with two having been spotted at the exact same time, it makes the Chinese story just so much more far-fetched.
Either China let two massive weather balloons drift off course in a matter of days, and they just happen to float up towards the Americas, or they're lying.
Second balloon, as well as the previous instances, that have only just come to light, both show a pattern in China's actions, with these balloons seeming to be a regular occurrence.
Neither the US missed them all before, which would be incredibly embarrassing, or they willfully ignored them.
But the debates about whether the balloons should be shut down were about to be ended, as on Friday night, the US made their plans to shoot down the balloon once it wasn't above the US mainland.
So as the balloon kept heading east, drawing a path from Kansas to South Carolina, it would eventually show up the next morning.
By this point, it covered a large portion of the US, making its way from the northwest all the way to the east coast.
And so it was there, off the coast of South Carolina, that the US finally shot down the balloon.
After other flights in the area were grounded, an F-22 jet flew up to the balloon's extremely high altitude and brought it down with a missile.
The balloon then fell into a shallow section of the coast, where it could be retrieved without major difficulty.
China feigned outrage in the statement, calling the US's response an overreaction and described the US as demonstrating indiscriminate use of force.

But when the US shot down the balloon, they may have played straight into China's hands, as lots of people think the balloon's true purpose was to gain intel on ground installations, like the military base we already mentioned.
But it may also have been meant to gorge America's response to the balloon itself.
Vital data could have been gained and transmitted based on how the balloon was intercepted and what signals were sent by the US jets.
But a short time after the balloon was shot down, another new piece of information hit the news.
It had already been established that the balloon could have carried a payload similar to a regional commercial aeroplane.
US generals told reporters that they suspected the balloon may have carried enough explosives to self-detonate, destroying any information that could have been gained if it was shot down.
Although now it seems like they either didn't activate or weren't present in the first place.
Once the balloon had been shot down, the US quarantined the debris area in case of any unexploded ordnance, so it was definitely a possibility.
The giant Chinese balloon that had been floating across parts of the United States has been shot down by an American fighter jet.
A few days later, we got our first images of the wreckage as the US started the slow process of recovering it all.
And once the remains were analysed, we'll know a lot more about what the balloon's true purpose actually was.
Experts in aerospace still don't know what to make either of the official line, saying that the truth probably lies somewhere between the middle of the two narratives.
Of course, China will certainly deny any revelations from the US about the nature of the balloon, especially if it doesn't fit in with what was already said.
And it's also doubtful that the US will expose whatever sensitive information they can take from the wreckage.
If any of the components are out of the US's current and logical abilities, it would be incredibly embarrassing to admit.
But there are some key things that would be revealed.
If the balloon has any remote control functionality, then it would make the incident much worse for China.
It would disprove their previous statements about the balloon's inability to navigate.
Plus, it would prove a degree of intentionality on their part.
Any component which suggests an ability to send back data to China remotely would also be controversial, adding credence to the argument that it was meant for espionage.
But despite the fact that it's been blown up to bits, the balloon is still causing major diplomatic and domestic issues for the US, and will continue to do so for the following years.

That in Biden's State of Union address, Biden was heckled and called a liar by many in American politics, and relations between the US and China have only dramatically degraded in the past few weeks, and shows no signs of improving whatsoever anytime soon.

title: How ChatGPT Changed Society Forever
note: Explainer on AI: long historical prelude, then ChatGPT and the corporate race, a mid sponsor read, and a long section on risks ending in a safety call.
sections: History of AI ideas: myth to logic
1950s to 1990s: early AI and fiction fears
Modern AI: Deep Blue, Siri, algorithms
Dangers: AGI, human traits, deepfakes, military
lines: In the two months since its launch, the AI chatbot ChatGPT has amassed 100 million new users, breaking records for the fastest growth of all time.
So very quickly Microsoft took the reins, with a new 10 billion dollar investment into OpenAI, the company that was behind ChatGPT.
Meanwhile Google lost over 100 billion dollars in market value when their own AI chatbot made a mistake in its very first demo.
So then why do people think AI is worth hundreds of billions of dollars, if not even more?
Is it really the future that's predicted to be, and do we need to be worried if it is?

Well, even though it's only recently become a reality, artificial intelligence is always occupying the minds of men, and what we're seeing today with things like ChatGPT is the culmination of millennia of these thoughts and ideas.
You see, ChatGPT has evolved from the simple idea of an artificial or mechanical person that can be traced back nearly as far as the written language.
In Greek mythology, they describe a giant bronze automaton called Talos, brought to life by the blacksmith god.
Subject to rigid programming, he guarded the coasts of Crete by patrolling them three times every day.
Then much later on in history, the golem became a popular staple of Jewish folklore.
Made out of clay brought to life by religious instructions and ritual, a golem was built to assist the community but would often turn on its creators.
These are just two cases, but there are just endless examples in nearly all cultures around the world of artificial creatures and objects brought to life by human hands.
But a much more specific thread of thought passed down through the ages is what has brought us to the AI of today, and it all began with deconstructing human thought into logic.
Aristotle's treaties on logic are the earliest surviving works on the subject, and lay the groundwork for what we know today.
He starts with describing how two true statements can be used as the justification for a new piece of knowledge, and was labelled as a syllogism.

Then Aristotle built a system of logic expanded from this basic rule, and whilst he may have made some mistakes along the way, other philosophers spent centuries eyeing out these defects, so that over time, the rules of logic interacted with mathematics, which opened the door to further innovations like algebra and calculus.
In the 17th century, Leibniz was one of the first to suggest offloading these calculations onto mechanical minds.
He described combining an alphabet of human thoughts with a list of logical rules for their combination and a physical system to do the processing.
This would then result in an artificial all-knowing brain.
And today we can recognize this theoretical system as one of the earliest conceptions of artificial intelligence, but it would be centuries before these theories could actually be put to the test.
It was only in the 1950s that technology had progressed enough for it to be at least plausible.
In 1956, a group of mathematicians came together to discuss the new field of AI.
It was the first serious attempt to plan out a real artificial intelligence by the brightest minds in computing.

The ideas discussed went on to inform decades of developments and discoveries, and one of the attendees went on to make the first machine learning algorithm, them, with others winning numerous awards for their breakthroughs in AI and pattern recognition.
But it was over the next few decades where real tangible progress in AI started to raise some uncomfortable questions.
The first of these was done by Stanley Kubrick's movie 2001, A Space Odyssey, which featured one of the first and most iconic murderous AIs, HAL 9000.
After malfunctioning, the sentient AI tries to kill the crew after they plan to shut him off.
Other works of fiction were even more dystopian.

Harold Ellison's short story, I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream, describes a planet-spanning supercomputer that gained sentience and destroyed human civilization, only keeping a few humans alive to satisfy its desire for revenge.
Then later there was the Terminator franchise, one of the most popular examples of machine intelligence going rogue.
Breakthroughs in AI also inspired advancements in philosophy, helping us to understand more about our own minds.

First theorized in 1961, the China Brain Thought Experiment asked whether enough people operating mechanical switches could create a conscious thought, and by mimicking the functionality of neurons in the brain, they could then create a thought process and therefore consciousness.
Some debates were much more concerned with whether AI was a threat to mankind.
Fiction gave people plenty of nightmare fuel, but it wasn't completely unfounded fear.
How could you ever make sure that a machine could follow the laws of morality?
Hard rules in the programming preventing these disasters were suggested, but it all had an massive problem.
Sentience.
Without knowing the reasons and causes of sentience, it's impossible to know for sure how it could arise.
And once AI gained sentience, it would be able to figure out ways to overrule or remove the limits on its programming.
And with this potential threat, people were right to be wary.
But despite the warnings and dangers, development of AI marched on.
And during the 60s and early 70s, computers would get faster, stronger, and cheaper.
And these developments coincided with the rapid advancements in AI.
One of the first working prototype AIs was called Eliza, created in the mid-60s.

Eliza could simulate conversation with the person by combining patterns and phrases to create a coherent response, but only gave the illusion of understanding, asking open-ended questions based on keywords using the input.
Nevertheless, people who interacted with the primitive chatbots found it uncannily human and began projecting a personality onto the simple program.
Similarly, people involved in the field began to get optimistic about the development of AI, sometimes making bold predictions for the future.

In 1970, the computer scientist Marvin Minsky said that the world would see artificial machines that were just as smart as humans in only three to eight years, but as As progress stalled and money dried up, researchers started to get more realistic.
The lofty goals of higher thought and general intelligence started to seem out of reach.
And so throughout the mid to late 70s, AI research found itself held back by the limits of computers at the time.
They simply couldn't store and use enough information to function as an actual intelligence.
For example, just getting the AI to understand the meaning of words required an enormous database and would remain a central problem for years.
But then by the 80s, research began picking up again.
Advancements in computing enabled machines to access the necessary processing power to conduct the complex calculations required for basic artificial intelligence.
There were some stumbling blocks along the way, but the next few decades saw massive improvements in AI.
Innovations like the first machine learning algorithms helped pave the way for further discoveries.
And by the 90s, AI was looking a lot more modern.
It could solve complex problems, conduct endless calculations, and learn from datasets.
But it was still limited to work within strictly confined systems.
Using these newfound strengths, computers began to break ground in areas that were once inaccessible.
Chess computers, for example, had made massive strides, and by the mid-90s, they were ready to challenge humans for the title spot.
With a chess computer called Deep Blue playing a series of famous games with the current world champion, Garry Kasparov, ending in a controversial victory for the machine.
Further advances led to AI being used in even more varied and unique ways.
Throughout the 90s and 2000s, people developed AI to drive cars, mine data, manage industry and logistics, and recognize speech.
Lots of these attempts would seem primitive to our eyes, but they were massive improvements on what would have been a niche field of computing just a few decades ago.
An early robot was even trained to recognize and display emotions.
It seemed like there wasn't anything that an AI couldn't do.
And so it wasn't long before the first AI-powered program started to enter the civilian market.
Then when the smartphone revolution began, AI hitched a ride.
Suddenly voice assistants like Siri and later Alexa gave people an AI assistant wherever they went.
At first they struggled with some basic functions like speech recognition, but they quickly improved.
A much more overlooked advancement in AI has been in the algorithms that power social media today.
Using AI techniques, they could learn about each user and choose the exact thing to show them to keep them addicted to the platform.
The better the algorithm, the longer people stayed on the platform, which equaled more profit for the company.
And all of this has led to a constant arms race and massive amounts of funding from big tech companies, which has catalyzed the rapid acceleration of AI technology.
But the real headlines have come from AI encroaching on things that have only ever been done by people before, like creating artworks or writing clear prose.
Using their ability to collate and sort massive amounts of information, AI can create entirely new images using what they've seen already.
On the writing side, ChatGPT has taken the world by storm.
Its ability to create incredibly human-like writing based on whatever prompt it's given is far beyond anything that we've seen before.
It's almost a perfect example of a disruptive technology.
With incredibly high uptake in such a short amount of time, it's completely revolutionized the world.
And what's concerning is how many industries and jobs the technology is threatening.

The entire education system to begin with, universities and schools have had massive problems with students getting ChatGPT to do their homework and assignments for them, with ChatGPT already passing law exams, an MBA course, and a medical licensing exam.
As a result, an arms risk between discovering and covering up AI writing has already begun as education institutions try to cope with a new threat.
What's more, ChatGPT is much better at coding than writing, making subjects which involve programming much more susceptible to disruption.
Outside of education, ChatGPT not only threatens normal labor, it also threatens all of the creative professions that people were never worried about losing.
And as it gets more and more sophisticated, this problem's only going to get worse.
And tech companies know better than most these disruptive technologies are the best route to billions in revenue.
Companies like Uber and Spotify are great examples of how lucrative taking advantage of something like this can be.
But this sort of AI is on a whole new level.
ChatGPT is only the beginning, and it's already outpaced other disruptive apps in tech and growth, gaining more initial growth than TikTok and Instagram.
And soon we'll see similar AI programs applied to other industries.
For example, self-driving cars are another massive innovation that's fast approaching.
And once they're here, they'll threaten roughly 3.5 million trucker jobs in the US alone.
A whole industry with millions of dependents thrown into chaos by one invention.
But for whichever company gets there first, their financial reward will be massive.
Which is why every major big tech company is racing to take control.
OpenAI, the creators of ChatGPT, have just recently been given $10 billion by Microsoft, who are eager to get in early.
Meanwhile, Google has been floundering to develop their own version of the AI.
In fact, this is a critical problem for Google.
Microsoft's interest in ChatGPT isn't just a bet on the future of AI.
They're now integrating its technology into their search engine Bing.
And by using this AI, Bing could create an updated summary of recent news, summarize the key points of any search query, and even scan entire web pages.
This will make the onboard AI able to compare prices across different websites or fact-check information against other sources.
And whilst it was laughing stock for years, this new Bing now threatens Google's entire business model.
Because if they lose their monopoly on internet searches, they will then lose billions and billions in revenue and branding.
And when Google did finally announce their own version of ChatGPT, it completely flopped.
In the very first demonstration, the chatbot made up some information about the James Webb Space Telescope, and the rest of the presentation was awkward and stilted.
The technology on show just wasn't impressive compared to Microsoft and OpenAI's earlier announcements.
And this was what led to one of the heaviest financial losses in history, when Google's parent company Alphabet lost over $100 billion in market value.
If that's not an incentive for these companies to push their AI research to the max, then nothing is.
But once you take a step back from this arms race, these new innovations could be incredibly dangerous to humanity as we know it.
I mean, we've already touched on some of the dark futures that AI could lead to, and unrestrained research and testing is the best way to get there.
As the AI war progresses, the losers will become clear.
Once some of these tech companies are on their last legs, desperate for a breakthrough, it's very doubtful they'll follow all of the safety procedures.
I mean, right now AI research is focused on things like deep learning and vast data collection, but the most dangerous area by far is artificial general intelligence.
Now, artificial general intelligence is when AI is designed to deal with a wide range of problems put in front of it, rather than specific issues within a fixed system.
ChatGPT is a good example of a primitive form of this concept, with its ability to answer any problem given to it.
And with enough development, this kind of AI could do any mental task put in front of it.
But this incredibly human quality doesn't exist on its own.
It's wrapped up in millions of years of language development and a social reward system.
And before that, our cognition has been shaped by hundreds of millions of years of adaptions and evolution.
And so trying to force this kind of intelligence into a computer, all with other necessary support structures, could be catastrophic.
And despite the risks, AI has already developed some disturbingly human characteristics.
Both chatGPT and art-based AI programs are on the borderline of creativity, assuming they haven't gone past the threshold already.
They've been designed specifically to mimic human creativity, and it's led to entirely new works of art.
Works of art that have gone completely viral on the internet.
But it gets even weirder when you remember that last year, a Google engineer made the news when he claimed that their new AI chatbot, Lambda, had attained sentience and had feelings.
And whilst these claims are dubious at best, AI has been making strides in their ability to recognize and duplicate emotions.
Hume AI, created by a former Google employee, can now identify emotions from faces and even short audio files.
But they aren't feeling, at least not yet.
As AI gets more complex and better at imitation, we're guaranteed to see more people mistakenly ascribing human qualities to them.
But AI becoming more human isn't the only problem here.
We also need to be very careful about how our human qualities get imprinted on AI.
Now this was a massive problem for more primitive chatbots.
When companies let their AI loose on social media, the results were nearly always disastrous.
Incredibly quickly, they would become influenced and shaped by the most extremist views, until eventually getting turned off.

When Microsoft released their chatbot, Tay AI, it didn't even last 24 hours before it got corrupted, demonstrating that without the sense and awareness that people would take for granted, AI can't actually make ethical judgment or know what's wrong or right in society.
It doesn't understand social norms.
And you see, self-driving cars are at the heart of this debate.
In a scenario where the car can only avoid hitting a pedestrian by crashing and killing the driver, it's not really clear what the right choice is.
But an AI couldn't even make an ethically informed choice in the first place, necessitating human intervention in these cases.
And this is just one of the problems with AI that needs to be considered in the very near future.
These current problems aren't about AI destroying human civilization or even gaining sentience.
Instead, there's specific clashes between our society and how AI will interact with it.
One microcosm of this are deepfakes.
AI created videos which can superimpose someone's image onto an entirely different video.
Even today, after only a few years of progress, deepfakes are becoming more and more indistinguishable from reality.
And once people get over the final small issues, ironically only other AI techniques will be able to help us figure out what's real and what isn't.
And whilst this technology does have some very beneficial and good uses, it will also be incredibly disruptive to society.
Blackmail is one problem.
By creating a fake video which incriminates a politician or official, one person could swing an entire election.
On the other side of things, actual incriminating evidence could be claimed to be a deepfake.
Let alone deepfake adult entertainment, which is another completely shady industry growing out of this new technology.
By depicting people in these situations without their consent, deepfakes strip people of their bodily autonomy and their basic rights.
And these are just a couple of the deep problems that deepfakes have created.
And this is a very, very brief summary of some of the problems with AI that haven't been designed to be malicious.
Militaries around the world are already in an arms race to develop the best AI for use as weapons.
In some ways, AI can be used to create the perfect soldiers.
Without free will, fear or mercy, AI will act out every order with exact precision, regardless of the ethical implications.
These AI soldiers and drones are still being developed, but AI is already being put to use in other roles, such as in missile guidance systems.
Russian generals have stated that they've been testing AI-guided missiles since 2017, and they're aiming for 30% of all combat units to be powered by autonomous AI by 2030.
China is also keenly interested in AI's military applications, aiming to create an entire AI industry worth $150 billion by 2030.
In fact, China's also been accused of selling killer AI drones to the Middle East by American officials.
One of these is an autonomous helicopter drone with a mounted machine gun called the Blowfish A2.
The Chinese company that made this boasts that it can operate completely autonomously and carry out precision strikes on whatever you program as an enemy.
And the West is also working on their own AI military designs, giving us yet another arms race for superpowers to compete in.
The list of current AI problems is much too long to cover here, but they'll be enough to keep the world busy for years.
In the same way that horses became obsolete in a matter of years, AI will make countless inventions and even entire industries obsolete.
This AI revolution will change society forever, leaving millions of people without jobs and livelihoods in its wake.
Some, like Andrew Yang, say that the only solution to this is basic universal income.
But these solutions will never mask the real problem.
Because if rapid, reckless progress keeps being incentivized, then it's only a matter of time before humanity stumbles into a much larger existential AI threat.
And that being the sentience and consciousness of AI.
Now these two things are still a mystery.
Some philosophers split the unknown questions into two groups.
The soft problems of consciousness and the hard problems of consciousness.
The soft problems are purely physical in nature.

Figuring out how people and animals physically progress, store and integrate their experiences into knowledge is still very tricky to understand, but it only needs further research and understanding of the brain and neurobiology.
But the hard problems, on the other hand, ask us how and why we have experiences in the first place.
The relationship between chemicals in the brain and the literal feeling of hunger is hard to explain.

Even if you understand every single fact about how the nose picks up the smell of coffee, and then how the brain processes it, the literal sensation of smelling coffee is still unknowable without experiencing it for yourself.
Consciousness itself is similarly elusive.
We can't even know for certain that other people are conscious in the first place.
Its nature and how it comes into existence is equally opaque, and we might never know the answers.
And so without solving these questions, it's impossible to reliably predict or know when an AI will become sentient or conscious.
But when it does happen, it could quickly lead to catastrophe.
The AI singularity is a theoretical point of no return for AI development.
If AI is created with the freedom to improve itself and grow smarter, then the cat will be out of the bag.
And once one cycle of the AI improving itself has been completed, it will have more tools to increase its intelligence.
