The cycle will then accelerate exponentially, as will the intelligence of the AI itself.
And once it surpasses human levels of intelligence, we'll have no idea what the results will actually be, as we won't know what its overall goals are, or its values and how it will act.
You could equally see humanity as a threat, an ally, or it might not even care about us at all.
You could throw off the limits and checks that we have implemented, or misinterpret them entirely.

And that's why some like Elon Musk suggest that the second solution to this deep-rooted problem is to actually integrate ourselves with AI by inserting brain chips into our consciousness to become fully symbolic with AI and join forces.
And as creepy and dystopian as this sounds, Elon Musk's fears of AI taking over humanity are based in reality.

I mean just imagine this for example, if humans create a super intelligent AI doing something as simple as creating paperclips, this mundane purpose could quickly spiral into chaos as the AI would see humanity as an obstacle in its eternal quest.
and by destroying human society and changing the world into a sprawl of paperclip factories, the AI would still only be working towards its meaningless goal.
Our destruction would ultimately just be a side effect.
And so it should be clear to all of us that we have absolutely no idea what we're really dealing with.

title: Coca Cola’s Darkest Secret: The Disturbing Truth
note: Corporate exposé of Coca-Cola: origin via Candler, marketing and war-driven growth, rivalry, then a list of alleged harms, with an early sponsor read.
sections: Hook: from mediocre drink to empire
Sugar addiction and hiding the truth
Plastic pollution and plan B drugs
lines: At the start, Coke was just a copy of a much better and more popular drink called Vin Mariani.
Despite Coke containing a mixture of cocaine and caffeine, it sold poorly by any one knew about it and it was about to be forgotten forever.
But then, in just 10 years, one man used shady business tactics and some of the most advanced psychological marketing techniques to turn this drink into a global sensation.

And now, 100 years later, Coke has become an international empire of exploitation, with the drink company now being accused of funding paramilitaries to assassinate union leaders in Colombia, sucking the poorest villages dry of water, making the most vulnerable addicted to their products, and actually getting rid of their toxic waste by giving it to poor people as fertilizer.
So how did this nameless mediocre drink become a global coke cartel?
Coca-Cola's origins as the company we know today begin with a man named Asa Griggs Candler.
He was a drugstore owner back in the day when drug prohibitions weren't really a thing, with drugs like opioids, cocaine, cannabis being as free and readily available as coffee.
So when Candler met fellow drugist John Pemberton and tried his carbonate to cocaine caffeine mixture, he immediately knew there was massive opportunity here.
But Pemberton had been having trouble selling the product, despite his addictive qualities.
So he tried to market it as a health product, but after years of trying, it never really got him anywhere.
Kandler knew Pemberton was an easy mark as well.
Having been wounded in the civil war 20 years before, Pemberton had himself become addicted to morphine to cope with the chronic pain.
His addiction had left the man in poverty, making him desperate for money in his final years.
And so Kandler understood that this tragic figure was sitting on a gold mine, so he pressured Pemberton to sell his formula and his share of the rights to the company.
Pemberton, with one foot in the grave and hoping to leave something for his only son, agreed to a measly price of just $2,300.
With Pemberton dying just one year later, he would never know what his drink would become.

In fact, according to stories from the time, Canler finished his buyout of Coca-Cola when he bought the rights to the name from Pemberton's widow for $300, a deal which he made at Pemberton's funeral, with his widow eventually dying just days later in a mysterious house fire.
And we'll never really know the true details here.
Kenner had all the records of the old company destroyed a couple decades later to cover his tracks.
But no matter what, Coca-Cola's origins were tragic.
But now that Pemberton and his ideas of a health tonic were out of the window, Kenner was finally free to turn Coke into a real product.
At this point, Coca-Cola wasn't being bottled yet, it was still just a syrup.
Pharmacists would take deliveries of the syrup and dilute it with carbonated water, selling the resulting liquid for 5 cents a cup.
And by 1892, Cannon had taken this business model over and was ready to give it the boost it needed.
But at first, he struggled with the same issues that Pemberton had.
Low sales.
People just weren't very interested in Coca-Cola to begin with.
In fact, the drink averaged just 9 sales a day.
But two things were about to launch Coca-Cola into the stratosphere.
And the first of these was advertising.
Cannon knew the product was sound.
You can't get a much more addictive product than cocaine and caffeine mixed together.
So Cannon understood that the main thing that he needed to do was market the product to the masses.
And this is when Canla began the first mass advertising campaign of Coca-Cola's history.
Through a relentless torrent of billboards, newspaper ads, coupons, and even signs on the back of horse-drawn carriages, Coca-Cola became impossible to avoid.
The ads often focused on health benefits, but the most effective ones simply branded the drink as delicious and refreshing.
After this campaign, sales immediately went through the roof, enabling Canla to expand the business indefinitely.
But another factor was pushing Coca-Cola to new heights, and it really had nothing to do with Canla at all.
You see, the late 1800s were the beginning of a craze in America for a movement called temperance.
Alcohol was seen by these people as a moral evil and something to be avoided entirely, which eventually led to legislative prohibition.
As the movement grew, organisations like the Anti-Saloon League pushed people out of bars and taverns.
But the movement paid no attention to the drug cocktails that pharmacies were selling.
In fact, they were seen as a healthy alternative, which meant that instead of heading towards the saloon after work to get drunk, workers would actually go to the pharmacy to get high.
And when they got there, they found their cocaine and caffeine-infused Coca-Cola on sale for just 5 cents a cup.
And after their first pop, people just couldn't stop.
The product was ridiculously addictive.
And so in just three years, Coca-Cola was soon being drunk in every state in the US.
And just 10 years after taking over the company, Canada's sales increased from 9,000 gallons of syrup a year to over 370,000 gallons.
At this point, Coca-Cola had firmly implanted themselves in the minds of Americans.
But there was now a growing pressure to remove the cocaine.
So after 1903, they started processing the coca leaves to remove most of the cocaine.
Although trace amounts were still present until 1929.
So Canada needed something to keep people drinking coke.
So we turned to a different, highly addictive white powder.
sugar.

Now today we all know too well the incredibly addictive and unhealthy qualities of sugar, but even just a few decades ago, this wasn't the case, and it certainly wasn't widespread knowledge in the early 20th century.
It was this new combination of sugar and caffeine that spread like wildfire when mixed with Coca-Cola's massive focus on advertising.

And to put into context, by 1911, Coca-Cola was spending over a million dollars on advertising every year, the equivalent of 31 million dollars today, and it was this magic formula that would remain unchanged for the next century, catalyzing Coca-Cola's growth to the top.
Over the years, Coke would perfect their marketing schemes and their ability to co-op trends.
It's a common misconception that Santa Claus was green before Coke made him red.
In fact, Santa was wearing red decades before Coke's first advert.
Although their first attempt at festive advertising in 1931 was incredibly successful for Coke.
And over the years, more ad campaigns would shape Santa's image to fit their purposes.
At first, it helped Coke because people thought of it as a summer drink.
So Santa helped convince people to nurse their coke addictions all year long.
Later on, Coke's relentless Santa marketing pushed the whole holiday away from religion and towards secular consumerism.
Before, he was small enough to fit down people's chimneys and was much more elf-like.
So Coke made him taller, fatter, and gave him a big white beard.
And as Santa advertising ramped up, this image slowly replaced all the others.
Saint Nicholas the Saint was being replaced by Coke's Santa.
And this consumerist new version of the Saint worked perfectly to target children.
Like the tobacco company selling candy cigarettes, Coke was making sure the next generation of children would be addicted to their products.
All until 1919, when Candler eventually sold the company for $25 million.
And considering he only bought it for a few thousand just a few decades ago, this was one of the most lucrative deals in history, and the new owners were ready to bring Coke to the world.
Over the 1920s, Coke became widespread in places like the UK, France, and later Germany, and their sponsorship deal for the 1928 Olympics helped strengthen the brand internationally.
But just like in the beginning, Coca-Cola were always ready to exploit any opening they could find.
And that was when Coke came to Germany around 1929, in which they exploded in popularity.
And by the time that Adolf Hitler had come to power in 1933, sailors were already at 100,000 cases of Coke a year.
Still a modest figure, but a clear foothold.
And if Coke wanted to dominate the competition, they needed to have a strong foothold on all the countries in the world.
And so they embraced the new regime, happily complying with Nazi regulations.
In fact, they eagerly supplied huge amounts of Coke to the 1936 Berlin Olympics, and later sent sales teams to Nazi political rallies.
Even when the war started, Coca-Cola didn't want to lose their market.
They tried to skirt trade embargoes for a time, but eventually they weren't allowed to import any more syrup to the fascist nation.
So instead, Coke would make a new drink called Fanta, using waste products that were common in heavily rationed Germany at the time.
Even when every other food and drinks were heavily rationed, Fanta was still everywhere.
And by 1939, there were 43 bottling plants in Nazi Germany.
and later on in 1943, there were 3 million cases being sold in Germany alone.
But once the war ended, the Coca-Cola company fell back into place and completely stopped production of Fanta and went straight back to Coke again.
But playing both sides wasn't the only way Coca-Cola profited of the war.
In fact, World War II was one of the best things to happen to Coca-Cola as when war was declared by the USA in 1941, Coke was ready and waiting with a genius marketing move.
It was going to be costly, but Coca-Cola's president at the time made an announcement that every serviceman would be able to buy a Coke for just 5 cents a bottle.
Now by doing this, Coke would lose a ton of money, rolling out the infrastructure necessary for this.
But eventually, in the long term, this was going to be worth it.
It would make the entire US addicted to Coke.
And it allowed the company to send Coke around the world.
Where the troop convoys went, Coke followed.
Then the US government got involved, helping Coca-Cola set up even more overseas factories and infrastructure with taxpayer money.
They even let Coca-Cola field special representatives in US military uniform.
These so-called Coke kernels spread Coke to the entire military, and the soldiers helped spread it to the local population.
And so by finding this opportunity in World War II, Coke had given themselves an international distribution network, partially funded by Uncle Sam.
And over the next few decades, the emergency wartime factories and bottling plants were converted into permanent civilian operations.
Everywhere the US had been, Coke gained a foothold.
They used them to spread into the rest of the world.
And in a world that wasn't really used to high sugar diets, it was like Coke was still using the old cocaine recipe.
Even though Coke was still absolutely massive in the USA and was still growing, international expansion started to outpace domestic gains.
So by the late 1950s, overseas sales made up a third of revenue and Coca-Cola had spread to over 100 countries.
This was helped along by Coke's signature brand focused advertising.
You see, unlike traditional marketing, Coke's always focused on making sure that the brand name and logo were omnipresent.
Simple Logans and scantily clad pinup girls were often the only things in the advert.
And it was this strategy that had worked so well in the US that helped cement Coke's name abroad.
Meanwhile in the US, Coke was always innovating on advertising.
Their advert, I'd like to buy the world of Coke, was possibly the most groundbreaking advert of all time.
By exploiting cultural shifts, their international presence and a focus on brand over substance, Coke had then made one of the best adverts of all time.
But not all of Coke's marketing techniques have been so obvious.
Now, despite their claims to the contrary, Coke has been working on covert techniques in order to get kids addicted early on.
Their co-option of Santa Claus is just one part of this.
Other cuddly Coke mascots like the signature polar bears help toe the line.
However, Coke ads don't appear on specifically directed children's TV.
Oftentimes, this is against the law, so Coke has always had to think outside the box to get kids addicted, which is why Coke targets things like theme parks and even schools.
In fact, Coke is found in school vending machines around the world.
Coke specifically signs contracts with schools to ensure that they only sell Coke's products in place of healthier alternatives.
Some schools are even offered bonuses based on how many Cokes they sell to children, incentivizing the education system to addict as many children as possible to Coke.
And by taking advantage of how underfunded and poor so many schools are, they have then secured the next generation of Coca-Cola addicts.
And Coke is also constantly lobbying governments to either keep the status quo in check or even extend their reach.
I mean, leaked emails between top Coke executives have revealed Coke's grand strategy to beat new sugar taxes and get past the flimsy red tape.
All of these measures are designed to instill a lifelong sugar addiction in children, with Coke even going as far as buying out Columbia pictures just to get around advertising laws.
Just recently, a whistleblower has released staggering new information on the death of Coke's conspiracy.
If the American obesity rates were listed on the stock exchange, everyone would be buying, as they've steadily increased ever since mass sugar consumption began.
Today, over 40% of Americans are obese, and a further 30% are overweight.
But there's a reason that people keep getting fatter whilst nothing changes.
You see, it's much more profitable for food and pharmaceutical giants to sell quick-fix band-aid solutions instead for the very problem that they're creating.
The American Academy of Pediatrics, which decides prescription guidelines for the entire country, has recommended that everyone over 12 who's obese should be prescribed medication.
severely obese children should also be put in for bariatric surgery, the complications of which can be life-threatening.
Unsurprisingly, the American Academy of Pediatrics is mostly funded by the same pharmaceutical companies who sell the medication.
And Coke actually rigged the system by paying off the American Academy of Pediatrics to pay the American Diabetes Association to silence facts on how damaging Coke really is for children.
For example, did you know that once they blacked it so that Coca-Cola got recommended to children?
Like, kids can drink Coca-Cola, it's good for you.
But there was competition now.
The only reason people don't pay attention to Coca-Cola's monopoly is that it's a two-horse race.
Pepsi started later than Coke and struggled to gain ground on the giant at first.

Multiple bankruptcies during the early 20th century meant that they were playing catch-up for decades, but they finally began to even the playing field in the 1960s after a lucrative merger, and the market share started moving in their favour.
But lots of the new Pepsi customers were former Coke customers, and the rise of Pepsi was costing Coke their entire monopoly.
Then later on, the competition got even more direct in one of the greatest campaigns of all time, Pepsi created the Pepsi Challenge.
The idea was to showcase people choosing Pepsi over Coke after a blind taste test.
And it worked.
By 1983, Coke's market share had been significantly eroded.
It looked like Pepsi was going to overtake Coke once and for all.
So Coke needed a dramatic response.
And this is when they launched their ad campaigns calling out Pepsi, resulting in the rivalry known as the Coke Wars.
Now clearly any ad that convinces a Pepsi customer to switch brands would be a win for Coke and vice versa.
But there was a second reason Coke and Pepsi were happy to slug it out in newspapers and on TV.
By only talking about each other, both of the companies make it seem like there are only two options, Coke or Pepsi.
In these terms, the other competitors aren't even worth talking about.
It's not collusion in the traditional sense, it's still an adversarial relationship, but it does help ensure the survival of both brands and their monopolies.
However, despite this, Coke's falling market share was historic.
Coke had never faced such a struggle before, and if they didn't do something fast, Coke could soon become irrelevant.
And so eventually they found their perfect solution in a new product.
So-called new Coke was sweeter, cheaper to make, and beat the Old Coke and Pepsi in blind tests.
Diet Coke was also sucking away regular Coke's customers, so it looked like the traditional beverage was on the way out.
So Coke's upper management made the drastic decision of phasing out Old Coke entirely.
Within months, new Coke was everywhere, and Old Coke was finishing production.
However, this backfired almost immediately.
After years of ad campaigns and cultural entanglements, the sudden absence of Old Coke led to outrage, and suddenly sales dramatically dropped.

Which is why only a few months after the decision, Coke walked it back and started making Old Coke again, with New Coke dwindling in popularity, eventually being renamed and then completely discontinued.
The only legacy it left was a failure and a warning not to try and fix what isn't broken.
Paradoxically though, while New Coke was a complete failure, it did give Old Coke a much needed boost once it was reintroduced.
This rubber band effect was so big that people even accused Coke of framing the whole thing as a marketing stunt.
But there's not really any evidence for this.
However, even with this disaster, Coke's overall market share was over 40% and it stayed in this dominant position all throughout the 90s and 2000s.
And it was from there that they cemented their position at the top of the industry.
Which is why by the 90s, Coke's market share was now over 40% and has stayed in dominant position ever since.
Along with Pepsi, they control a massive global monopoly on soft drinks.
But now that they've scaled up to the highest position possible, the company now only faces two problems, maintaining their monopoly and suppressing the truth about their product.
Because just like the tobacco industry and drug cartels, Coca-Cola's empire has been built on addiction.
In fact, a 2008 study on sugar's addictive potential gives us the unsettling truth.
It examined four main attributes that make something addictive.
Patterns of binging, withdrawal symptoms and cravings.
That's why when rats were exposed to sugar intermittently, they developed all three of these behaviours as a result of changes in brain chemistry.
And those same processes that occur from dopamine abuse from hard drugs are also very present in sugar consumption.
The global addiction was harder to detect when the effects weren't so obvious, but they are becoming obvious now.
Skyrocketing obesity rates over the past few decades have made it harder to ignore.
However, Coca-Cola always had a plan for this.
Along with other big players in the food and drinks industry, they worked for years to hide the truth about sugar addiction.
That's why all these big sugar companies like Coke have always pushed the narrative that fat is the real problem to health, not sugar.
And despite little evidence for these claims, it became an accepted fact.
Lobbying and getting friendly with government officials have sealed the deal.
And when people finally began to catch on after all the low-fat products didn't really work, Coca-Cola moved on to denying it entirely.

They pumped millions of dollars into research that cherry-picks examples to try and prove that there's no causation, and once these stilted and biased studies came out, Coca-Cola then used them to argue against the obvious health consequences of sugar, with the end result of all of this being a massive loss in the quality and duration of many people's lives.
Obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cancer are just a few of the very dangerous side effects of Coca-Cola's products, conditions which have taken decades of life of millions of people's life expectancy.
These negative health effects also disproportionately affect impoverished people who don't have much of a choice or the education to know what they're getting into.
But to maintain their monopoly, Coke has had to do more than just protecting their addictive product.
Their more recent history has been characterised by a pattern of snuffing out potential competitors before they can get a foothold, with Coke destroying local competition by any means necessary.

lines: Silicon Valley Bank, one of the largest banks in the United States, went entirely defunct in just 48 hours.
So how did the 16th biggest bank in the US lose everything so quickly?
Well, SVB Bank is the warning sign that we are now in an appending recession.
Just like Lehman Brothers' collapse, SVB is going to be the catalyst for a worldwide recession.
So what led to the unprecedented collapse of one of the United States' largest banks in just a matter of days?
Well, you see, after seeing massive growth through the initial phase of the pandemic, SVB began tumbling during the start of 2022, until it hit zero the very next year.
Now it's not uncommon these days to hear talks of imminent financial collapse, but it's another thing entirely to see it happen to a massive investment bank like this.
And now the bank's implosion has obviously not gone unnoticed by their customers, as over 1,500 tech companies could be facing huge financial problems because of SVB's downfall.
Additionally, around $20 billion in funds have been entirely wiped from banks in Canada after a continent-wide sell-off of SVB's stocks.
So then the real question here is where did this massive sell-off of SVB stock come from?
Well, over nearly four decades of business, SVB had found their niche acting as a middleman between venture capitalist companies and the startups they invested in.
You see, when a startup found itself with millions or billions in investments, they would always put it into Silicon Valley Bank.
And over the course of 2020 and 2021, the markets for tech companies and startups were booming, attracting massive investments in new companies and projects.
Silicon Valley Bank quickly saw their assets skyrocket from just under $70 billion to nearly $210 billion.
So in the span of just two years, they got three times richer.
But with so many deposits being made, the bank had an entirely new problem.
You see, they were quickly running out of loans to give, which was how they usually made their money.
And without new loans to keep up with their new billions, they had to turn to another way to use their new money.
So they started putting their money into securities, financial products designed to be sold off in years or decades after purchase.
And doing so would net SVB a guaranteed profit, as long as they didn't sell them too quickly.
And if they did, they would have to sell them at market value.
And the executives at SVB bit hard on these securities, putting a reported $70 billion into them.
But at the time, no one really cared, and everything was looking great going into 2022.
The bank was the richest it had ever been.
So what could possibly go wrong?

A third of their assets had just $15 billion of their value.
So selling them would be absolutely disastrous.
Furthermore, these interest rates were extremely bad for tech startups.
and this was SVB's main clients who had given them their billions in the first place.

Many of the key firms working with SVB advise companies to withdraw their money from the institution, and recommendations such as this are about as bad as it can get from a bank.
These type of suggestions will almost suddenly lead to bank runs, which, unfortunately for SVB, immediately happened after the news of their financial decisions and subsequent losses went public.
Now, for those who don't know, bank runs occur when a large number of customers believe a bank will fail, and deposited money starts being withdrawn in droves.

So with SVB's recent report and selling securities at a loss, and their attempts to liquidate company stock, it's really not hard to see why the majority lost faith in the institution and started to cash out.
Customers began withdrawing their money from SVB so fast that the bank became insolvent in just a matter of hours.
In fact, the police were even called to stop customers withdrawing their money.
However, given SVB's financial state and investment decisions, there was absolutely no chance the bank could pay their debts they owed.

And so then just in a few days, SVB had a negative cash balance of almost a billion dollars.
And like most banks, SVB keeps only a small portion of deposits on hand, while investing the rest of their funds into whatever they see fit.
However, SVB had even less collateral after putting 91 billion into these awful securities, leaving them incredibly vulnerable.

It's hard to understand how they could have made such a risky, stupid decision.
Usually there's a whole department dedicated to managing risk, specifically so that this sort of thing doesn't happen.

It was left without anyone in charge for the nine months before the collapse.

This kind of self-policing corruption is all too common in the financial industry.

people like ex-royal couple Harry and Meghan will report to lose millions that they had in the bank.

And when you look at the cause of the collapse, where a ton of dangerous securities lost their value, and it all starts to seem a little bit too familiar.
SVB may have thought they were being more cautious by buying more US treasury bonds compared to other banks, but this is what caused their downfall.
