lines: The New York Times has completely lost the trust of the people.
It used to be one of the most trusted newspapers in the world, being one of the only media companies uncovering government secrets and reporting the truth.
But today they've completely lost it by shoveling their own hollow political agenda.
It's things like censoring offensive words from Wordle like wench that makes you ask, what really happened to the New York Times?
Because you see, back in the day, the New York Times was never a propaganda tool.
You see, in the early 1900s, the paper found its footing by telling objective truths without opinions and sensationalism mixed in.
They gained a reputation as a serious record of history, which would further help them find their footing when the newspaper industry shrank and large conglomerates started dominating the market.

And so by the 70s, the New York Times was ahead of the pack, selling over 250,000 tons of newspapers every year, as they made their perfect brand through honest reporting and delivering the truth to the world, whatever the cost.
And nothing proved this more than the Pentagon Papers scandal.
In 1971, the New York Times gained access to classified documents on a secret study of the United States' involvement in the Vietnam War, And they didn't shy away from the truth.
They released it to the public despite the harsh legal consequences they could incur.
They even transmitted the story through a satellite system which would spread it around the world in a matter of moments.
And the US government really wasn't happy.
This was like an early version of WikiLeaks, so they tried to punish the journalist who broke the news with charges of conspiracy and espionage.
But it just didn't work.
More leaks then revealed a smear campaign by the government to implicate the journalist on false charges, leading to the entire case being dropped and the New York Times skyrocketing in popularity.
People love their unapologetic honesty in the face of authority.
The New York Times even won a Pulitzer Prize for their work on the Pentagon Papers.
But this success would eventually lay the groundwork for the collapse we're seeing today.
Because the US government really wasn't happy about having their dirty secrets exposed.
But then they couldn't go after the paper or the journalist directly.
There were just too many pesky freedom of the press laws to get past.
So if they didn't destroy the free press, maybe they could directly control it instead.
Long story short, it worked.
Individuals have had to step in when news organizations have failed.
Today, when they expose massive government conspiracies, they're not given awards.
They're jailed for life or forced into exile.
Just look at Edward Snowden and Julian Assange.
They played the same role the New York Times did when exposed government lies.
But this time, they didn't have the same protection.
They were banished from the country, with the CIA even trying to assassinate Julian Assange.
But then this brings up the question, if things like WikiLeaks were exposing the government, what are media outlets like the New York Times doing these days?
And how do they actually make their money when the whole newspaper industry is completely dead?
while the answer to these questions lies in the early 2010s.
You see, as we all know, as the 21st century began, print newspapers started to decline and fast, as the switch to online media was killing thousands of small papers.

In fact, from 2005 to 2021 alone, over 2,000 US newspapers collapsed, which meant the larger newspapers like the New York Times also suffered as well, because the fact that online news was free and instantly accessible destroyed their physical sales.
They only survived by moving to a paywall subscription model, which already has its own problem.
But even this really wasn't enough, so the New York Times sacrificed the one thing that they had left, their objective, hard-hitting, authentic reputation.
So from 2010 to 2015, the paper started printing more and more of these left-wing articles and opinion pieces, even though they acted like they were completely non-partisan.
And you can start telling this by the types of words that cropped up in their articles.

I mean, just over this five-year period, articles that mentioned social justice roughly doubled, mentions of whiteness more than tripled, and articles talking about diversity and inclusion became more than six times as common.
And it didn't hurt that this shift also matched the owner's interests and agenda.
You see, the New York Times is mostly owned by the Olshbergs family, a family at the top of New York's pyramid of liberal elites.
But then when you dig a little deeper, you'll find the exact same names that are always pulling the strings.
Companies like BlackRock and Vanguard, who also own large shares of the paper, mounting to over a billion dollars in investments between the two.
Now this trend towards a corporate, hollow, woke, leftist bias can be seen across the board.
but it's particularly egregious for the New York Times, as their focus on objectivity and truth makes this shift just even more jarring.

Now, this wasn't really new to anyone, though, and it's all part of what Noam Chomsky described as manufacturing consent, as they saw this growing shift in the media towards a corporate narrative, rather than just left or right.
Because as a seemingly objective news organization, the Times' responsibility is to document history.
But by letting these corporate interests in, like BlackRock and Vanguard, buy out huge portions of the paper, they've then let them exert influence on the paper's opinions.
They can choose what's talked about by the paper and which issues receive the most coverage.
And it's through these invisible tools that they can then change the narrative of history to suit their own elite agenda.
For Chomsky, this is what he calls the propaganda model of communication, as he describes the ways that media companies have become the voice of corporations and the government.
And one of the first points they bring up is that these media companies are driven by profits.
This means that they will say whatever makes their owners money.
For the New York Times and their subscription model, this mostly means pleasing their left-wing audience.
But only to a certain extent, natural left-wing doctrine that could threaten Black Rock Vanguard or all the other elites is rarely ever seen for this reason.
Anything going against big tech, big pharma is never discussed again.

And this is when economies of scale work against the people, because the media industry has been taken over by a few massive conglomerates that have preferential access to the stream of global information.

And someone always has to tell the news companies to fax, and these usually come from government sources, which means that any news company that steps out of line can be starved of relevant new information.
And this would lead to a loss of audience and revenue.
This would lead to a loss of reputation, giving the government even more leverage over the media, not to mention all the big companies that can withdraw their investments.

In fact, governments and corporations even hire people to complain and make a scene over stories that don't fit their narrative, damaging the media company's revenue and reputation which forces them to always capitulate, along with the continued threat of always losing their investors' money if they step out of line.
And so it's through these ways that the media is pushed towards certain narratives, and it's how they manufacture consent for the status quo.
And for the New York Times, this is especially true.

And that's why today, there's this repulsive special brand of corporate liberalism that's taken hold, the one that places all of its attention on dividing people by their identity and paying lip service to diversity and social issues without ever actually changing anything at all.
In fact, these are the people that wanted to maintain the status quo, and that created the societal trends that the New York Times seems to supposedly hate.

However, this move towards corporate bias did have some real benefits for the paper, as it helped them keep hold of their loyal audience of old, rich, left-leaning readers, who always agree with the agenda of the elite.
But for a more general audience across America, it wasn't a very welcome change, because as the more biased the New York Times got, the more people they alienated.
Instead of appealing to general America, they were now dividing America.
And then on top of this polarisation and revenue issues, suddenly the New York Times had a recipe for disaster.
Which is why unsurprisingly in 2014, the New York Times had to fire over 100 of their newsroom employees.
And if nothing changed here, the paper likely would have continued its slow roll into mediocrity, relying on a dwindling number of long-time readers.
But instead they were given a lifeline, something which would boost their ratings and would provide endless news for years to come.
Now, despite how much they professed to hate Trump and everything he stood for, the media like CNN and New York Times just couldn't get enough of him.
During the Republican primaries, it's estimated that Trump was given $2 billion worth of free coverage from the mainstream media, which is roughly six times what his opponents received.
And they didn't just help him indirectly.
Lead tapes revealed CNN's president encouraging Trump to run for president and even giving him advice on how to win a CNN debate.
Ironically though, one of Trump's core platforms was always stoking resentment against the left-wing corporate mainstream media.
And after he did this, the media started to turn on him.
But he attacked the media for a reason.
They were insulting and being condescending to the unrepresented and alienated people that the coastal elites were scoffing their noses at.
With Trump in office, the New York Times were given four more years of division and political polarisation to work with.
So, they exploited it, pushing their editorials and actual reporting further and further left.

but as they committed more to the BlackRock style of corporate leftism, they started running some real problems, as it's tricky to mix real factual reporting with an ideology that doesn't reflect reality, and the cracks were starting to show.
However, on the surface, things seemed great, as winded into Trump's administration, and the New York Times' revenue soared by 10%, with their stock price rising by 20%.
And by increasing the polarization and taking more money from their loyalist fanbase, the paper made their shareholders a lot richer.
But despite record profits, the paper's true value, its reputation, was under serious threat.
In June of 2017, they had to fire all of their copy editors, over 100 staff.
Then they graciously let them compete for 50 different jobs at the paper.
And this would be a grave mistake, as copy editors were the ones fact-checking and proofreading articles before they were published.
And this is crucial for any news agency to get the facts right, especially for the New York Times, which used to pride itself on having the best accuracy in America.
And yet at the same time, they were also firing fact checkers and instead hiring agenda pushers.
One of these new appointments in 2018 was Sarah Jong, a new member of the editorial board.
And it didn't take long for her history to surface.
Just hours after her hiring was announced, people started bringing up these tweets where she broadcasted her hatred.
The defense for this was that these tweets were contextual and meant to satirize other racial abuse, but it was weak.
The Times had hired and fired another writer for exactly the same thing just months beforehand.
The only difference was who her comments were towards.
This double standard showed the growing bias of the New York Times, a culture of cancellation for past tweets if it didn't match their agenda.
And this was one of the signs that they were moving further away from honest reporting and more towards pushing the corporate agenda.
Another sign came in 2019, when the Times published a political cartoon depicting the Israeli Prime Minister and Trump.
The only problem was that it was anti-Semitic, especially concerning the caricatures, and also the use of the Star of David in the cartoon.
And it bears mentioning that a copy editor would have noticed this, but they were all fired.
Even though the New York Times is supposed to be one of the least racist, most woke, and progressive media outlets out there.
And then instead of just retracting the cartoon and apologizing or just moving on, they got rid of all political cartoons permanently.
And so a method of challenging the establishment that's been used for centuries is now gone from the Times.
And it isn't hard to see who benefits from this.
This is the real reason the corporate leftist agenda is pushed so hard.
It restricts free speech against authority.
And with Trump in office, it isn't just cartoons either, the Times has been getting rid of any articles which don't match the narrative as well.
A year later in 2020, the Times published an opinion piece by Senator Tom Cotton, which advocated for the use of military force as a backup to stop out-of-control riots.
People on the left reacted badly, decrying the Times' commitment to showing both sides of the argument.
And at first, they defended themselves, bringing up the logical point that you need two sides to a conversation to even know what you're arguing against.
But it didn't take long for a motion to win out over reason.
And a few days later, the New York Times threw in the towel, striking the article from the record and apologising for ever publishing it.
But this flip-flop spoke to a great attention within the paper's management over how far they should toe the party line.
After they removed the article and went back on their commitments to journalism, the senior opinion article's editor resigned.
And over time, people who fight back against the encroachment of corporate ideology are now being removed one by one, leaving a news agency full of hollow puppets.

People have started to notice though, and it's doing irreparable damage to the New York Times' reputation, which is why you might see some reception to their propaganda like comments saying this, And Magic April has more validity than the New York Times.
Or this comment which came directly from one of their YouTube posts.
Calling them out as quote, misinformation peddlers.
Quite a contrast from their God and reputation just a few decades ago.
And we're already seeing how this narrative driven reporting has damaged the Times' ability to report the truth.
Like for example, when people rightfully doubted the official narrative on COVID origins, the Times would be quick to push back.
But they championed this bull animal transmission theory with very little evidence.
as they would be very quick to fall in line with the who and the government narrative.
And to make sure it stuck, they also tried to discredit the lab leak theory, dismissing it as this far-right conspiracy.
But then fast forward to today, with the lab leak theory being the most probable cause of COVID, and then the New York Times suddenly tried to push the blame on Dr.
Fauci in a very shameless opinion piece.
And whilst Dr.
Fauci was massively complicit in this, the New York Times was just as complicit.
But then why are they pushing this narrative in the first place?
Well, it's just another example of public opinion tampering.
By suppressing the truth for years, the New York Times took all the blame off of China until the heat had died down and people moved on.
And this isn't the first time.

They've pushed all sorts of narratives to help China's narrative, which speaks to the New York Times no longer being an edgy paper, but a paper for the elites, for authoritarian governments, and for the World Economic Forum.

But for all their grandstanding about leftist doctrine and protecting people, the New York Times is just as greedy and ruthless as any other massive corporation, with the exact same agenda as BlackRock.
For example, the New York Times had previously bought out the tech review site Wirecutter.
Just like with Wordle, the business side of the agency had seen that it was a promising website, and so they bought it out whilst keeping it mostly independent.

But they then used this independence to justify far lower wages for the employees, and other opaque decisions from upper management, like when they put a paywall on the site in 2021, forcing it into the same subscription model that the Time users.
However, it was only after most of the company went on strike that they were eventually forced to pay them competitive wages.
Then it came out that the Wirecutter management had been accepting what they called kickbacks for good reviews on the site.

Now whilst the New York Times didn't own Wirecutter when this was happening, it still reflected poorly on them when the news broke later on, as this was the sort of corrupt upper management that was plaguing the New York Times itself.

Every day, more and more people are waking up to these failures of the New York Times as a news organization, with Elon Musk in particular attacking the paper for their awful reporting, calling their feed diarrhea and saying that their propaganda isn't even interesting.
Even other news outlets have seen the blood on the water.
The Spectator ran this article titled The New York Times Blunders Again and Politico were on it years ago, where they ran this article asking what happened to their reputation for unbiased reporting.
And we all know the answer to this.
So is it really only one that they lost their checkmark on Twitter?
Now this corporate agenda that seeped into The New York Times isn't really unique.
It's a worldwide phenomenon.
And whilst wokeness is the most visible symptom, it helps to distract from the narrative control and silencing that comes with it.
And that's the real purpose of the shift, to make profit and distract from what's really going on behind the scenes.
And it's also why the New York Times' reputation for telling the truth is all but gone.
They're just another puppet of the establishment.
But if you want to see what happens to real journalists today who exposed the system, just take a look at what happened to Julian Assange by clicking the video above.

And as they pushed voting messages to their more liberal audiences, it was found that they were able to convince more and more people to vote for liberal parties, with YouTube having a 76% chance of showing you a liberal video over a conservative one through autoplay.
And now they're using AI to push this narrative as well.
OpenAI's ChatGPT has a liberal corporate bias based on the data it was programmed with.
And even if just a small subset of people start using AI to get that information, then whoever controls their AI will easily be able to shift public opinion to their favor.

And by hiding behind their AI, Google and Microsoft will be able to control information even more than they do now, in addition to the World Economic Forum, international governments, and major corporations.

title: How Apple's Vision Pro Will Change Society Forever
note: Opinion essay in the form of a problem-first argument about one product: hype, what it really solves, how it was built, then societal harms with philosophy references.
sections: Real world web and societal changes
lines: Apple's new Vision Pro terrifies me.
On June 5th, 2023, Apple released their brand new game-changing product, the Vision Pro, and the hype was unreal.

In just the buildup to the new product announcement, Apple's stock was bubbling up, rising in anticipation for its release, because Apple's leadership and key investors knew that by invading their new Vision Pro, they would be changing human history forever.
Because as soon as the product was announced, everyone everywhere was quick to say that this was the same as when the first iPhone was introduced, or the first Mac.
The Vision Pro is being praised by all corners of the internet and media.
But this feels like the Series Zero, like the Apple Watch.
Remember when the Apple Watch first came out?
The Series Zero.
The parts of this headset that I tried are actually the best I have ever seen in any VR headset by a mile.
This headset is claimed to be the ultimate mixed reality VR AR experience.
And I will say, it may very well be.
When they're boasting the ability to recreate the world around you in real time using LiDAR scanning and TrueDepth cameras from the headset you're wearing while it supposedly runs cool and quiet?
Man, even at that price point, I'm pretty blown away.
Everyone in the dog knew that this was the beginning of a new era.
Tweets everywhere praising Apple's holy grail, their most addictive, cutting edge and groundbreaking piece of technology yet.
To the point that even huge companies like Disney, partnering with Apple due to their strong conviction that this will finally be the VR headset to make virtual reality mainstream.
With Bob Iger, Disney's CEO, saying, And we believe Apple Vision Pro is a revolutionary platform that can make our vision a reality.
And they're not entirely wrong.
This is most definitely a groundbreaking, historic, and unprecedented product.
But throughout all of the noise, one question has stuck with me about all of this.
What problem is Apple actually solving?
Now, this is the fundamental question of all businesses, because every great product is built from this line of thinking.
What is the problem?
How big is the problem?
And how can I solve this problem?
The bigger the problem and the bigger the solution, the more money you make as a business.
If it's a million dollar problem, the solution makes millions.
If it's a billion dollar problem, the solution makes billions.

Jeff Bezos with Amazon, for example, if it solves the issue of a shop not having the products that you want, having to go to different shops for different things, the hassle of actually going to the shop in the first place, going at certain hours, having to stand in line, whilst Amazon also provides cheaper prices than any other shop with instant delivery.
This, along with all the other problems that Bezos is solving through Twitch, Whole Foods, Audible, Blue Origin, etc, has made Bezos one of the richest people in the world.
So then this brings back the question, what problem is Apple trying to fix with the Vision Pro?
Well, at first it seems like they're just trying to solve the issue of virtual reality not being popular in the public.
But is this actually a problem?
Does anyone actually want virtual reality to be mainstream, apart from Silicon Valley tech elites?
No, the real problem that the vision pro is trying to solve is that not everyone in the world can have everything they always want.
In fact, for the average person around the world, you have almost nothing you actually want or need.
The despairing malaise that hangs heavy in the West permeates from the fact that there is no sense of adventure in your life, no community, no freedom.
You spend every day struggling to pay the rent, the bills, the debt.
Prices keep increasing, taxes keep hiking, your income is stagnating, a recession is booming.
Where we live in dystopian citadels with trans inhabitants, squabbling cheek by jowl for space.

where your only free time is spent being shuttled on grindy-slope-packed public transport through a dangerous urban sprawl, with just enough energy left at the end of the day to mindlessly watch a drip-drip of lethargic, empty entertainment.
where you then wake up in a gloomy, claustrophobic tower block, streaked with grime and riddled with moss, provoking the moral decay of your atomized existence.
And as bleak as this may sound, this is the average life for most people, but with the perfect virtual reality system, this problem is solved.
If the product is good enough, then the sad reality of your life just slowly fades out and a new reality begins.
You can be crying of loneliness in your dark, empty apartment, but then when you put on the headset, your true reality just dissolves away.

You're taken to see different friends, different cultures, different places, different memories, more social media, more dopamine-sucking videos, more games, more pleasure, in a way that you've never experienced before.
I mean, when Tim Cook announced the Vision Pro, one of the key aspects of this new technology is the idea that this new kind of computer will blend the real world and the digital world together.
A process that has already been catalyzed by Apple today.
I mean, when you just stop and look around you, you'll notice how many people are just completely consumed by their iPhones and Macs.
Our attention spans have been decimated by iPhones.
The design of the iPhone and how addictive it truly is has kept the average person in a perpetual cycle of destruction ever since, endlessly disrupted by short dopamine hits.
That's why in 2022, it was calculated that the average American can spend six hours a day on their phone and another four hours on their computer.
But with the new Vision Pro, you won't ever need to pick up a phone or a laptop.
You can just be plugged straight into the Appleverse with your eyes, attaching your own consciousness, your life, your business, your culture, your society into a virtual world run by Apple.
I mean, already we saw this in 2021 with Meta's metaverse, as companies like Nike were buying up virtual shoe companies, along with Walmart, McDonald's, Gucci, and just so many more.
But then you may be asking, what is actually the problem with any of this?
What's so bad about it?
Surely this isn't something that negative.
And even if it is, it's very unlikely that it's going to be widely adopted.
I mean, the Vision Pro is $3,500.
People don't have the money to be doing this.
Most people don't even make this in a month.
No average person's going to have the money to be doing this, right?
Well, trust me when I say that the rabbit hole of the Vision Pro goes so much deeper than you first think.
And very soon, the Vision Pro will become as normal as MacBooks are today.
This is Apple's plan.
And to understand the true consequences of Vision Pro and what experts are terrified of, we need to see why the Vision Pro was created by Apple in the first place.

Now the idea for Apple's Vision Pro stemmed from the increasing interest and potential of augmented reality technology, with Facebook being rumored as early as 2013 to be putting all of their focus into virtual reality.
And with this knowledge, Apple knew that they had to have skin in the game because this wasn't just Facebook.
Companies like Oculus, Microsoft and HTC were already releasing their own VR headsets, creating a competitive landscape that Apple had to navigate.
Because Tim Cook and Apple's leadership knew that eventually phones and laptops would reach a cap in their market potential, but virtual reality was a completely new possibility.
Because eventually phones and laptops will reach a cap in their market potential, but virtual reality was a completely new possibility.
An untapped, highly addictive industry with the potential to change the entire global economy and human history.
Apple recognized the society-changing possibilities of blending the digital world seamlessly with the real world.
And time was running out.
They had to get started before any other company like Facebook monopolized the industry.
Because if Apple wasn't at the forefront of VR, then this could have potentially wiped out billions of Apple stock a decade later in the future.
And with Apple's strategic history of staying at the forefront of technological advancements, there was no way they were ever going to be behind Facebook in the VR wars.
Now, not much is known about the development of Vision Pro.
However, Apple has worked on the headset hardware and software since at least 2016, most likely 2015, in a division called the Technology Development Group.
However, as soon as development started on the Vision Pro, Apple was facing some giant issues.
For starters, if Apple was going to addict and plug billions of people into their virtual reality, the experience would need to be seamless, as close to true reality as possible.
Which was an incredibly hard challenge, especially considering this was almost 10 years ago.
The most powerful VR headsets at the time was the first version of the Oculus Rift, and the Oculus was heavy and uncomfortable for long periods of time.
It was ugly and it felt fake.
There was no possible way when you used the Oculus Rift that you would believe it was reality.
So Apple knew that if they were going to keep people constantly wired into their own virtual reality, they would need to change this.

They had to make the design a compact and lightweight headset with powerful processors, high resolution displays, advanced sensors, and efficient battery systems, as though you weren't wearing anything at all.
Apple was treading uncharted waters.
No one had ever done anything like this before.
And that's why reports suggest that Apple's engineers and designers spent years refining and perfecting the headset's features, focusing on comfort, usability, and immersive experiences for years.
And this was just the start, because augmented reality also requires intuitive and seamless user interaction.

So Apple faced the task of designing an interface that would allow users to effortlessly navigate the digital and physical worlds also while maintaining a natural and immersive experience, so natural that you didn't even realize you had it on.
And in addition, the Vision Pro also had to integrate seamlessly with its existing ecosystem of devices and services.

As one of the key parts of the Vision Pro was that you could connect your photos and apply the iCloud system to your eyes, as though all the stuff that you do on your phone was now just your true reality, because this would allow you to do the unthinkable.
Things like watching memories from five years ago as if you were there in the exact moment when it happened.
Along with being able to work wherever you are in the world, without even a computer, all your contacts, work documents, notes, videos, presentations and music, all stored away in your eyes.

And this wasn't just as simple as using the same software for iPhones, iPads and Macs, because Apple would need to build from the ground up a completely robust, perfect ecosystem of virtual reality applications and content to provide engaging and diverse experiences for Vision Pro users.
Having to make deals with Disney to be on the Vision Pro, along with countless other companies that still haven't been disclosed yet.
But eventually, it worked.
And after almost 9 years of development, the Vision Pro now looks to be one of the first successful attempts at Silicon Valley breaking into the virtual reality market.
By delivering an all-in-one augmented reality headset, Apple has paved the way for immersive and interactive experiences that were once only the stuff of science fiction.
Even Ready Player One, a film that was released in 2017, seemed unthinkable.
But now with the release of Vision Pro in 2023.
And this not only sets a new standard for augmented reality, but experts now also warn that this radical new technology will transform every aspect of society.
And this is where things get really crazy.
Vision Pro is creating an entirely new economy.
Virtual reality and AI is what experts predict to be a billion dollar or even trillion dollar industry in the near future.
And just like the dotcom bubble, markets are eating up this vision of the future.
Although So what's been sold as market salvation is actually growth in just 7 tech stocks.
Opportunities that are long overhyped and overpriced by the time we get to them.
In reality, every other company is sinking into the red.
Inflation still rages.
And even with a healthy 6 figure salary, many people are still living paycheck to paycheck.
Apple's new headset, while very impressive, is only the beginning.
It bears the markings of a 1.0 product, the first unperfected move towards a new type of device, a new wave of technology.

And with the Vision Pro announcement coming just five days after the release of the MetaQuest 3, which was Zuck's latest attempt at growing his metaverse plan, it's clear that everyone in Silicon Valley is pushing towards this.
And that's why we're seeing the creation of what people are calling the real world web.
Apple referred to this in their announcement, calling the Vision Pro the first device they've made that you look through rather than that.
Rather than using a device to pay into the virtual world, people have the virtual world overlaid onto the real one.
We'll interact with it every day through virtual screens, objects, places and people.
In short, the virtual world will have finally crossed the border into reality itself, and the Vision Pro's double 4k screens are already close to photorealism, making this future alarmingly close.
And like I mentioned, this will change everything in society.
Surgeons, for example, will see real-time medical information and possible problems when they're working.
In fact, people can be trained for nearly any job using AR assistance.
People with memory loss will be able to relive lost memories.
Schools and colleges will combine classroom settings with virtual reality.
That's why the Vision Pro will change the world just as much as the internet has.
But if left unchecked, there will be some serious problems.
These social media platforms are picking the next president, the next congressman.
They're literally picking and they have the power to pick so they will be controlled by the government.
That's why Professor Reid explained when talking about virtual reality that, quote, the ultimate aim is not just virtual reality or augmented reality, it's mixed reality.
It's blending the digital and the real world together.
And ultimately, this blend may be so good and supervasive, the virtual and the real become indistinguishable.
And the market for that is gigantic because whoever controls it will basically have control of your entire reality.
And then when you really think about it, if an entire new world, memories, life and culture is adopted into the virtual world, then who's actually controlling this world?
The same company using sweatshops with suicide nets in China?
The same company caught spying on all of its users with iPhones?
The same company that sends us any political opinions that don't fit into their ESG score?
It's clear that our free will will not be as free as we think very soon because we're becoming attached to the virtual world on autopilot and it's already happening.
Where our phones and computers are morphing into our second brains with all of our memories, personal tastes, secrets, hobbies, music, conversations all being stored into a virtual cloud.
But once we actually live inside the virtual world, when our entire society and culture exists in this virtual world, that's when we need to be concerned.
Because if the Vision Pro succeeds, it will be bigger than the iPhone.
And this leads on to one of the biggest problems where they are in the Vision Pro lie.
Augmented reality will remove the last few seconds of time between the impulse to follow the distraction and getting the dopamine reward.
They will push the digital world of distractions right into people's faces.
And this final wall between us and the digital world is crucial.
Instead of having adverts and notifications appear on your phone, they'll appear directly in your vision.

With augmented reality, technology will become even more demanding of your attention and your time, and Apple will use this to their advantage, plugging you into their addictive data harvesting system 24-7, giving them an untold wealth of information to sell.
But it goes the other way as well.
One of the most celebrated upcoming features of the Vision Pro is its insane eye-tracking capability.
With a set of incredibly detailed and intricate cameras, the headset will use eye movements as a key navigation device for the entire interface.
I mean, it's already been revealed that the headset will create a user profile based on how you use your eyes to focus on things and view your environment.
And this information is gold to advertisers and personality profilers.
By studying the data on the exact way that you perceive and see adverts, big tech will have even more tools to predict what you'll want next.
They'll be able to tell exactly how long each thing they show you keeps your attention and what draws you away, what sights distract you, what colors light up your brain.
And this will complement and work in tandem with the real world web, meaning that your every desire will literally be at your fingertips.
And it's in this way that augmented reality and the real world web brings us far closer to Nozick's experience machine.
Now, this is a classic thought experiment of a machine that offers you the best possible existence, complete bliss and pleasure.
The only cause that comes with this is that you won't want to ever be unplugged.
It detaches you from reality itself.
Even though it's literal heaven, lots of people won't accept being plugged in, as there's a value in reality that's unattainable from a simulation.
Or at least that's what the thought experiment suggests.
And this is exactly what the Vision Pro offers, happiness and a world of information and entertainment at your fingertips.
but we've already seen that this isn't bringing people happiness.
In fact, it's doing the opposite.
I mean, the majority of people in the West have access to luxuries that the lords and kings of history couldn't even dream of.
Hot showers, a diverse and delicious range of food and drinks, entertainment at a moment's notice.
But we're never actually happier.
We're more miserable, lonely, and empty every single day.
Because the happiness that augmented reality and the experienced machine promise is false.
The whole idea of this philosophical concept is that happiness isn't something that we should value above everything else.
It's fleeting when it's provided through distractions and hedonism.
Nietzsche's work on happiness gives us the real reason behind all of this.
People see happiness as the end result of a cycle of wanting something, then getting it.
But for Nietzsche, happiness isn't the end result of a process, instead it's a byproduct of the process as a whole.
It's the journey, not the destination.
The hard work of achieving your goals in life, both big and small, is where happiness really comes from.
And the problem with the Vision Pro is that it promises to get rid of all the obstacles that make the journey in the first place, pretty much removing the journey entirely.
And this will kill the small amounts of happiness left to take on the world.
Paradoxically, pursuing happiness as the final goal, as the solution to the masses' problem, means that people will never actually find real happiness.
Therefore, Apple isn't really solving the issue that it's trying to fix.
Outside of helping you to do a specific thing in a specific case, it will only serve as a distraction just like iPhones do.

It will reduce your attention span and make you easily distracted and less determined, which are the qualities that run completely counter to the cycle of achievement that Nietzsche describes, that happiness inhibitors.
It's a procrastination machine, leaving the masses more addicted, more distracted, more dopamine deprived than ever before.
It won't just be people based on virtual reality though.
The type of content we consume will also change to reflect the shortening of attention spans.
The short form content that's become so prevalent will evolve to fill the niches that AR leaves open.
They already play on experience.
Most short form content tries to provoke a single emotion in the quickest way possible.

So just think of one minute pet adoption videos that are playing on your heartstrings or the five second skits and jokes that won your laughter or other forms of short form content that give you multiple things to focus on at once.
Like a podcast clip with some satisfying imagery or some game footage all mashed together.
AI will then let these videos intrude on your other senses and give them a real presence, making them that much more immersive and therefore more addictive.
These horrible videos becoming seamlessly integrated into your actual world.
Another side effect that most people don't even discuss about this is how virtual reality is going to affect people in delusions.
People like other kids, furries, or TikTok reality shifters who think they're actually in the Harry Potter universe.
Virtual reality will only give these people the means to live out their delusions, turning their own worlds into what they want them to be.
Well, just imagine political echo chambers that come into reality manifest themselves in your living room.
Or a world of Instagram models and influencers and adult entertainment stars that will look more real than real.

Without taking off the headset or unplugging from the system, and you'll be under the illusion that everyone looks perfect, your dopamine will be fried, and any addictions you have to attractive girls on Instagram and other sites will only be doubled.
This is the future we're rapidly approaching, and Apple's Vision Pro is the first step in that direction.
A new virtual world that will strip you of your privacy, discipline, focus, freedom, and authenticity.
So long as our culture continues to offer nothing whatsoever of substance, authenticity, or meaning, nightmarish trends like the Vision Pro will only continue to proliferate.
And the sad fact is that the majority of us will jump in without even a second thought.

But the first thing you have to do is calibrate your eyes and there's a short calibration session, it's about two minutes and you're in.
And this is where the magic happens.
So basically, the eye tracking in this headset as it looks at your eyes and keeps track of where your eyes move around is the closest thing that I've experienced to like magic.
Like I don't, I normally don't call tech things sort of magical or surreal like this, but this was, even for a pre-release product, kind of unbelievable how well it does.
Immediately after its release, Apple's YouTube video on the Vision Pro achieved 20 million views in a day.
Everything on Trending was about the Vision Pro.

Twitter was packed with supporters drooling over Apple's latest gadgets, with influencers like Casey Neistat even claiming that he wants a Vision Pro for everyone in his house, including the dog, adding that the Vision Pro is the answer for his kids.

Every big influencer and media personality is licking their lips at the prospect of the Vision Pro.

Anyone anywhere can live inside their own digital universe mixed with their current reality.
As soon as you put the headset on, your grey, empty, dull existence turns colourful, bright and hopeful as you plug yourself into the Appleverse.

A place where you can meet new friends, work anywhere you want, do business, sell anything you want, go to different countries, catch up with your family instantly, travel across dimensions, do everything you've ever dreamed of.

Now you can sit down at the family table, looking at your family straight in the eye, all while watching Family Guy clips with subway surfers, or have any other distractions to ensure that there is never a moment in your life with any boredom.

There's no such thing as headphones for video, right?
There's not something I can carry with me that I can put on and it gives me the same experience I get when I'm watching my, you know, 50-inch plasma display at home.
And, you know, until somebody invents that, you're going to have these opposing constraints.

Whilst this is a small detail, it's something that has never been done before in Apple history.
The CEO of Apple always uses the product as they announce it to the public.
So why did Tim Cook never use the Vision Pro?

Questions like, is this product ever actually going to be mainstream?
I mean, Tim Cook won't even use it in the presentation.
And when Apple revealed the price of the Vision Pro, there were audible gasps in the audience.
Apple Vision Pro starts at $34.99.
It will be available early next year on Apple.com.
And yet Apple and everyone you see in the media and online is claiming that the Vision Pro will be the new iPhone.
But at this crazy price point of $3,500, surely no one can afford this kind of product with no utility.
It just seems like some gimmicky product like an expensive Apple Watch, right?
Well, that is what Mark Zuckerberg thinks.

Upon the announcement of the Vision Pro, Zuckerberg recently claimed Apple went with a high-resolution display, and between that and all the technology they put in there to power it, It costs seven times more and requires so much energy that you now need a battery and a wire attached to use it.
He went on to say, the announcement really showcases the different values and vision that our companies bring to this in a way that I think is really important.
However, at the end, he noticeably remarked, we being meta, innovate to make sure that our products are as accessible and affordable to everyone as possible.
And that's a core part of what we do.
And we have sold tens of millions of quests.
To see what they'd ship.
And it's a good sign for our own development that they don't have any magical solutions to the laws of physics that we haven't already explored.
With Zuckerberg implying that the Vision Pro is nothing more than exclusive products for a select few, far from a mainstream product.
But after really digging deep into the Vision Pro and Apple's future plans, I stumbled upon new groundbreaking information that terrified me.
And that's when I came to the conclusion that I do think that the Vision Pro is almost certainly going to be a mainstream product.
And that's why I want to show you Apple's true plan to make the Vision Pro a mainstream product, and what the future of the Vision Pro will look like when it's mixed with AI and Neuralink.
Or even what this will look like in authoritarian regimes like China, where Apple already works actively with the CCP to censor and block anything the Chinese government doesn't like.
And even in the West, where Apple has been caught spying on all of our iPhone photos, what will this look like for the Vision Pro?
Well, trust me, as I tried to answer these questions, things took a very dark turn.
Because when you pull the veil back on the Vision Pro, it's incredibly nasty.
But to understand the full reasons why, we need to begin with a simple question.
How on earth will Apple make the Vision Pro mainstream?
And what is Zuckerberg wrong about?
Why will the Vision Pro take over the metaverse?

But more importantly, the Vision Pro offers technology that you just can't find anywhere else in the market.

Since at least 2016 and possibly as early as 2015, Apple has been working on both the hardware and software in a dedicated division called the Technology Development Group, where Apple went on a hiring spree, recruiting VR and AR experts and acquiring all the relevant companies needed to fulfill their vision of an Apple virtual reality utopia, to the point that there were over 5,000 patents and extremely top-secret technical knowledge that has been accumulated over almost nine years, allowing Apple to create a device with a similar impact to the first iPhone.
But still, even with a revolutionary product design, how on earth are people gonna buy into Apple's virtual reality dream?

allowing this soft, high-quality new reality to emerge out of your depressing reality, where all your past problems gradually fades away.

Or to have the same advantages as your peers, you will feel an inherent need to tune into the Vision Pro.
As all your friends, community, religious groups, celebrities, businesses and shops all start to operate within it.
Just as we've seen with iPhones, MacBooks, and social media.
And once you experience the Vision Pro inside of an Apple shop, once you pop, you just won't stop.

They want you to beg to see what your life will be like in the virtual world, how much better your life will be, how the person that you've always wanted to be, your destiny is just awaiting you in the Vision Pro.
Apple will cater to all of your demands.
And once all of this buzz, all of this variety for the Vision Pro takes off, they will then make the product substantially cheaper with a non-pro version of the product.
But then even still, the most likely price of the non-pro version of Apple's Vision will still likely be around $2,000 at least.
So why would anyone use this instead of a MacBook or iPhone, which offer everything you need at a massively discounted price?

Why?
Reddit communities are going dark tomorrow in protest of Reddit's new pricing policy.
Well, it all started when Reddit began charging for API access.
From July 1st, Reddit plans to charge developers that require higher usage limits, 24 cents for every 1,000 API calls or less than $1 per user every month.
Now, APIs are the only thing that allows third-party apps to exist on Reddit.
I'm talking about third-party sites like Apollo, which allows you to read several posts, comments and other Reddit features into a separate interface.
And these apps generally come free of Reddit ads and contain actually more features than Reddit itself.
But now that Reddit is charging for API access, this will cost Apollo $20 million every year just to operate.
So of course, the creator of Apollo announced on Twitter that Apollo will officially close down on June 30th.
But it's not just Apollo we're talking about here.
Because of these insane prices, this basically means that all third-party apps and mod tools will all effectively be shut down by July 1st, 2023.
And it didn't stop there.
As one of the biggest subreddits, Explain to Me Like I'm 5 described, quote, API access isn't just about making life easier for mods.
It helps keep our community safe by providing important concepts to our users, such as whether or not they have a history of posting rule-violating content or engaging in harmful behavior.
